title: The Shift Promise
description: The Shift Promise: five commitments covering evidence, uncertainty, commercial independence, informed choice and respect for individual weight-management journeys.
keywords: The Shift Promise Five simple commitments. These are the standards we want a user to be able to hold us to as the platform becomes a live Shift Programme. 1. Evidence honestly We'll explain what the evidence supports without inflating trial results into personal guarantees. 2. Uncertainty honestly When evidence is emerging, incomplete or disputed, we'll say that clearly. 3. No profit-led treatment choice We won't tell you a treatment is better simply because it is more commercially attractive to us. 4. Your informed decision Our role is to help you understand and compare; clinical suitability and final treatment choices require appropriate professional input. 5. Individual journeys matter There is no moral hierarchy between lifestyle, medication, NHS care, surgery or maintenance routes. How this connects to the Shift Programme The Promise sits alongside our Editorial Standards, Clinical Governance and Commercial Principles. It is not marketing copy that disappears when someone becomes a paying member.

title: Surgery Comparison Centre 2.0
description: Compare gastric sleeve, Roux-en-Y bypass, mini bypass/OAGB, gastric band, balloon and ESG side by side across weight loss, reflux, diabetes, reversibility.
keywords: Home / Treatment Centre / Compare the operation — not just the headline weight loss. Surgery Comparison Centre 2.0 Compare the operation — not just the headline weight loss. Written and researched by Matt O’Brien, founder of Shift Some Timber. Sleeve, Roux-en-Y bypass, OAGB/mini bypass, gastric band, balloon and ESG compared across anatomy, weight-loss evidence, reflux, diabetes, reversibility, nutrition, recovery, revision and NHS relevance. Updated 8 August 20266 procedure typesX vs Y battleUK/NHS context There is no single “best bariatric operation”. A procedure that looks strongest for average weight loss may create a less attractive reflux, nutrition or permanence trade-off for a particular person. The comparison needs to look beyond kilograms. Procedures at a glance ProcedureTypeRelative weight-loss effectReversible?Reflux contextNutrition burdenNHS context Sleeve gastrectomy Laparoscopic surgery High No Can worsen or cause reflux in some people Long-term vitamin/mineral supplementation and monitoring required Common NHS bariatric procedure where specialist assessment supports it Roux-en-Y gastric bypass Laparoscopic surgery Very high Technically revisable but not treated as a simply reversible procedure Often considered favourable where significant reflux is a major issue Higher long-term micronutrient burden than sleeve; lifelong supplements and blood monitoring are important Established NHS bariatric procedure One-anastomosis gastric bypass Laparoscopic surgery Very high Revisable but not a simple reversible treatment Bile reflux is an important procedure-specific consideration Meaningful micronutrient/protein malabsorption risk; long-term monitoring essential Offered by some NHS bariatric centres; not universal Adjustable gastric band Laparoscopic surgery with implanted adjustable band Moderate Yes, removable Can cause/worsen reflux, regurgitation or swallowing symptoms No intestinal malabsorption, but diet quality and follow-up still matter Much less prominent in modern NHS bariatric practice than historically Intragastric balloon Endoscopic temporary device Low to moderate Yes, temporary/removable Can worsen reflux/nausea in some people No intestinal malabsorption, but adequate nutrition and structured follow-up still needed Limited/selective availability; not a routine substitute for bariatric surgery Endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty Endoscopic suturing procedure Moderate Potentially revisable/reversible in some circumstances, but not equivalent to simply 'undoing' a band May be preferable to sleeve in some reflux contexts, but individual assessment matters Lower malabsorptive burden because intestine is not bypassed NHS now describes ESG as a weight-loss procedure, but availability is not universal Procedure Battle Pick any two procedures Procedure A Procedure BCompare VS Big decisions that often change the procedure discussion Reflux Sleeve can worsen reflux in some people, while Roux-en-Y bypass can be a more attractive discussion where reflux is significant. This needs surgeon-level assessment rather than a website rule. Type 2 diabetes Bypass procedures have particularly strong metabolic evidence. Diabetes severity, medicines and individual anatomy still matter. Long-term nutrition All bariatric patients need follow-up, but bypass procedures carry a greater malabsorptive/micronutrient burden than purely restrictive or endoscopic procedures. Reversibility A gastric band is removable; sleeve removes stomach permanently. ESG avoids resection but should not be marketed as if it were a zero-commitment procedure. Recovery Endoscopic options generally recover faster than laparoscopic surgery, but procedure intensity is only one part of the decision. Revision Weight regain, reflux, malnutrition and device problems can all create revision pathways. “One operation forever” is not guaranteed. NHS assessment threshold NICE recommends referral for comprehensive bariatric-surgery assessment for adults with BMI 40 kg/m² or more, or BMI 35–39.9 kg/m² plus a significant health condition that could improve with weight loss, subject to the full guideline and specialist assessment. Lower BMI thresholds can apply for some ethnic groups. Referral is not the same as being offered a particular operation. That does not mean every NHS bariatric service offers every procedure. Procedure choice and local availability remain specialist-service decisions. title: NHS vs Private Weight Loss Treatment
description: Compare NHS and private weight-loss medication and UK bariatric surgery across access, waiting, choice, monitoring, aftercare, continuity and true 1/2/5-year cost.
keywords: Home / Treatment Centre / Wait, qualify, pay — or combine the routes? NHS vs Private Comparison Centre Wait, qualify, pay — or combine the routes? Written and researched by Matt O’Brien, founder of Shift Some Timber. Compare NHS and private medication or UK surgery across access, speed, choice, monitoring, records, aftercare, long-term cost and what happens when the first route is blocked. Updated 8 August 2026England NHS detailTrue-cost calculatorX vs Y engine NICE eligibility is not the same as immediate NHS access. NHS England is still implementing tirzepatide in phases. Specialist weight-management services can access the full NICE-eligible cohort subject to clinical approval and local resource prioritisation, while primary-care access is being widened by prioritised cohorts. Local ICB delivery models matter. At a glance RouteAccessSpeedChoiceMonitoringCost NHS medication pathway Clinical criteria + commissioned pathway + local capacity Variable; can be slower because access is prioritised/phased Choice can be constrained by NICE guidance, local commissioning and service model Clinical monitoring plus required wraparound support where applicable No private medicine fee; NHS prescription-charge rules vary by nation/exemption Private medication pathway Clinical assessment by a regulated prescriber/provider; no NHS commissioning threshold required, but licence/clinical suitability still apply Often faster if provider has capacity Potentially broader choice among licensed treatments, subject to clinical suitability Quality varies; safe services should independently verify information and provide appropriate review Ongoing private prescribing/medicine/service cost NHS bariatric surgery pathway Referral + comprehensive specialist assessment + local commissioned service Can involve substantial waits and staged assessment Procedure choice based on specialist MDT, service capability and clinical factors Pre-op MDT, surgery, structured postoperative follow-up and long-term monitoring No private surgical package fee Private UK bariatric surgery Private specialist assessment; clinical suitability still required Usually faster than NHS if surgeon/hospital capacity exists Greater ability to choose surgeon/hospital; procedure still should be clinically appropriate Package-dependent — surgeon, dietitian, bloods, emergency/revision policy must be checked Substantial one-off/package cost plus possible follow-up/supplement/revision costs Route Battle Compare any two routes Route A Route BCompare VS True private cost calculator Do not compare “NHS = free” with one advertised private monthly price. Put in the actual provider cost, setup/consultation fee and recurring extras. Private monthly treatment/service (£) One-off setup/consultation (£) Other recurring monthly costs (£) Time horizon1 year2 years5 years This is arithmetic only. It does not predict price rises, dose-dependent pricing, treatment duration or future NHS access. If you meet NICE criteria but cannot access treatment locally 1. Confirm what criterion/pathway you mean NICE clinical recommendation? Current primary-care cohort? Specialist-service referral? They are different questions. 2. Check the local ICB route NHS England explicitly directs patients to local ICBs because access varies by commissioned model. 3. Ask about specialist services Primary-care rollout restrictions do not necessarily describe the full specialist weight-management route. 4. Compare private only if sustainable Starting privately is not just the first month. Model the likely ongoing cost and what happens if price or income changes. 5. Protect continuity If you go private, make sure relevant information can be shared with your GP and that monitoring/side-effect escalation are clear. 6. Keep NHS route alive where appropriate Private care and NHS eligibility are not necessarily mutually exclusive, but transfer/shared-care is not automatic. How to vet a private medication provider Verify the pharmacy/provider Use the relevant regulator register. Do not rely on a logo pasted into a footer. Expect real verification Current GPhC/NHS commissioning guidance says prescribing high-risk weight-management medicines should not be based solely on an online questionnaire; information needs independent verification through two-way communication, records or GP/regular-prescriber contact. Ask who monitors you Know who the prescriber is, how follow-up works, when you can contact them, and what happens with significant side effects. Ask about GP communication A cheap provider that creates a completely separate medical universe can become expensive when something goes wrong. Check the support, not just the pen NHS tirzepatide pathways require wraparound dietary/behavioural care. Use that as a quality benchmark when assessing private services too. Beware instant prescribing If the service appears designed to get from checkout to prescription with minimal clinical friction, treat that as a warning rather than a benefit. title: Ozempic and weight loss: the UK distinction
description: Ozempic is a diabetes medicine. Its name has become shorthand for weight-loss injections, but the brand, licence and prescribing purpose still matter. Start with what you need treatment for, rather than the name you have heard most often.
keywords: Ozempic and weight loss: the UK distinction Prepared by the Shift Some Timber Editorial Team. Sources checked 3 October 2026; this is not independent clinical review. Ozempic is a diabetes medicine. Its name has become shorthand for weight-loss injections, but the brand, licence and prescribing purpose still matter. Start with what you need treatment for, rather than the name you have heard most often. What is Ozempic licensed for? Ozempic contains semaglutide and is licensed for adults with insufficiently controlled type 2 diabetes, alongside diet and exercise. Weight loss can occur during treatment, but Ozempic does not have a UK weight-management indication. Is it the same as Wegovy? The brands share semaglutide as an active ingredient, but have different licensed uses and product instructions. Wegovy is a weight-management brand. Sharing an ingredient does not make pens, doses or prescribing plans interchangeable. Can my GP prescribe it? A clinician can assess diabetes treatment and decide what is appropriate. Asking for Ozempic for weight loss alone is a different question from treating type 2 diabetes. NHS access also depends on the relevant pathway. This page cannot confirm an individual entitlement or prescription. What should I know about side effects? Digestive effects such as nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea can occur. Persistent severe abdominal pain needs urgent medical assessment; sudden loss of vision or rapidly worsening eyesight also needs urgent help. Discuss other medicines and any planned anaesthetic with your clinical team. Do not stop or adjust diabetes treatment because of a comparison page. What if I already take it? Keep following your own prescription. If you are concerned about weight, side effects, supply or whether treatment is working, take those questions to the clinician managing it. Record the product name, prescribed dose, dates and problem before making contact. Avoid sharing unnecessary medical details in public comments or general website enquiries. What should I ask if weight management is my main aim? Which licensed options fit my health history, rather than just my BMI? Who is responsible for prescribing and ongoing review? What is included in the full cost and what happens if I need to stop? Where can I get practical food and movement support during and after treatment? Your next useful step If you are exploring options, use the treatment comparison as preparation for a clinical conversation. If you are already being treated, My Timber can support ordinary routines and check-ins without asking you to change provider. It does not replace your diabetes team or prescriber. Sources and further reading Ozempic: UK product information MHRA: GLP-1 medicines for weight loss and diabetes About this guide General information for adults, not a prescription or an individual assessment. Product information and your own clinician’s instructions take priority. This update replaces an incomplete guide with medicine-specific information and direct sources. title: Treatment Finder Methodology
description: How the Shift Treatment Finder scores route relevance, uses adaptive questions, reuses Health MOT data and avoids presenting treatment relevance as medical suitability.
keywords: Home / Decision Centre / How the Treatment Finder works. Transparency How the Treatment Finder works. Written and researched by Matt O’Brien, founder of Shift Some Timber. The engine ranks relevance, not clinical suitability. What data it uses The finder can reuse information previously saved by the legacy browser questionnaire, if it exists on this device. The current Health MOT link opens a separate proposed blood-test guide and does not create that profile. Finder answers add context about history, preferences and previous treatment; they do not establish clinical suitability. How route scores work Each route starts from a transparent base score and gains or loses relevance points from explicit factors. For example, repeated regain, high appetite and high food noise raise medication relevance; higher BMI plus comorbidities raise NHS and surgery relevance; readiness for food and movement raises lifestyle relevance. Why a score is not a probability A displayed relevance of 82/100 does not mean an 82% chance that a treatment will work, be prescribed or be clinically appropriate. It only means that, within this site's decision framework, more of your answers point toward that route being worth investigating. Adaptive logic The finder may reuse an existing local questionnaire profile. If none exists, some health context is missing. Treat the output as general information, check the stated limitations and discuss clinical questions with an appropriate professional. Education gaps The finder asks how confident you are about medication, surgery, NHS and lifestyle routes. If you report low confidence, it recommends relevant reading before you make a decision. Eating behaviour Regular loss-of-control eating reduces the usefulness of a simple 'diet harder' interpretation and increases the importance of behavioural or eating-disorder-aware support. The finder does not diagnose binge-eating disorder. Local data Results are saved in browser localStorage as sstTreatmentFinder. No account or server sync is used in this release. No hidden 'best treatment' answer The engine is not designed to make Mounjaro win. It is designed to show why each route moves up or down for this person. Open Treatment Finder Health information General information, not individual medical advice. Where treatment suitability matters, the decision belongs with an appropriately qualified clinician. title: Decision Centre Methodology
description: How the Shift Decision Centre interprets UK obesity-treatment pathways, NICE tirzepatide criteria, NHS primary-care rollout and bariatric-surgery referral thresholds.
keywords: Home / Decision Centre / How the Decision Centre works. Transparency How the Decision Centre works. Written and researched by Matt O’Brien, founder of Shift Some Timber. The engine is intentionally conservative. It identifies pathways worth learning about; it does not make treatment decisions. NICE tirzepatide threshold The engine uses NICE TA1026's core obesity recommendation: initial BMI at least 35 kg/m² plus at least one weight-related comorbidity. For South Asian, Chinese, other Asian, Middle Eastern, Black African and African-Caribbean backgrounds, the BMI threshold is normally reduced by 2.5 kg/m². Primary-care NHS tirzepatide rollout NHS England is implementing tirzepatide in primary care in phases. The initial high-priority cohort uses BMI 40 kg/m² or more, adjusted for ethnicity, plus 4 of 5 specified conditions: type 2 diabetes, hypertension, cardiovascular disease, obstructive sleep apnoea and dyslipidaemia. This describes the initial cohort, not a complete current eligibility check. Later phases and local implementation can widen access; check your ICB’s current route. Specialist weight-management services Specialist services and local commissioning can use different routes from the initial primary-care cohort. NICE clinical eligibility therefore does not automatically equal immediate GP prescribing. Bariatric-surgery assessment The engine uses NICE NG246 referral criteria: BMI 40+ or BMI 35–39.9 with a significant health condition that could improve with weight loss, plus willingness to engage with necessary long-term follow-up. Relevant BMI thresholds are generally reduced by 2.5 kg/m² for the ethnic groups listed above. NHS Digital Weight Management Programme The NHS Digital Weight Management Programme in England generally requires age 18+, BMI 30+ (27.5 for some higher-risk ethnic groups), and diabetes, hypertension or both. Why we say “profile appears consistent” A webpage cannot confirm contraindications, pregnancy status, medication interactions, psychiatric/eating-disorder context, prior treatment history, local commissioning or specialist judgement. For that reason, the engine never displays “You are eligible” as a final clinical conclusion. Weight-loss scenarios Scenario outputs use arithmetic only. The site does not infer that losing 15% guarantees a particular blood-pressure change, diabetes remission or elimination of sleep apnoea. Sources NICE TA1026 – tirzepatide for managing overweight and obesity NHS England – interim commissioning guidance for tirzepatide NHS England – weight-management injections and phased rollout NICE NG246 – medicines and surgery NHS England – Digital Weight Management Programme eligibility No hidden recommendation score The tool does not secretly assign Mounjaro 92/100 and surgery 81/100. Route labels are based on explicit threshold/context rules documented above. Open Decision Centre Health information General information, not individual medical advice. Where treatment suitability matters, the decision belongs with an appropriately qualified clinician.

title: Medication Comparison Methodology
description: How Shift compares weight-loss medications, trial data, formulations, NHS access, side effects and convenience without turning ratings into treatment recommendations.
keywords: Methodology How the Medication Comparison Centre works. Written and researched by Matt O’Brien, founder of Shift Some Timber. Direct evidence where possible. Clear caveats where direct evidence does not exist. We compare licensed formulations, not just molecules Semaglutide now exists in multiple UK products and formulations. Injectable Wegovy, oral Wegovy and Ozempic should not be collapsed into one row because indication, dose, evidence and access differ. Trial averages are anchors, not forecasts We use pivotal or head-to-head trial results to anchor relative efficacy. Individual results vary, trials have different populations and durations, and cross-trial comparisons are inherently weaker than head-to-head randomised evidence. 2026 Wegovy caveat The classic STEP evidence is built around injectable semaglutide 2.4 mg. UK product information now permits 7.2 mg weekly for weight management in adults with obesity if needed after at least four weeks at 2.4 mg. A historical Mounjaro-vs-Wegovy head-to-head using 1.7/2.4 mg semaglutide should therefore not be presented as direct evidence against 7.2 mg. Oral Wegovy Oral Wegovy 25 mg has its own OASIS 4 phase 3b evidence. We do not infer that daily 25 mg oral semaglutide is equivalent to 2.4 mg or 7.2 mg injected semaglutide milligram-for-milligram. Ratings We present study findings and practical differences without numerical treatment ratings. Separate trials are not a head-to-head ranking, and a study average is not a personal forecast. NHS accessibility This is deliberately conservative. NICE recommendation, NHS commissioning, phased rollout, specialist-service restrictions and local availability can differ. Prices We do not freeze a “typical private price” into the core comparison because UK private prices change frequently by provider, dose and supply. Future commercial pages should fetch or regularly review price data rather than fossilising it in a medical guide. Core evidence anchors Mounjaro SmPC / SURMOUNT programme Wegovy injectable SmPC / STEP programme Wegovy 25 mg tablet SmPC / OASIS 4 Saxenda SmPC / SCALE programme NICE technology appraisals and NHS medicine guidance No automatic winner. A medicine can have stronger average weight-loss evidence and still be the wrong choice for an individual because of contraindications, tolerability, preference, access or maintenance. Return to Medication Comparison Centre Health information General information, not individual medical advice. Where treatment suitability matters, the decision belongs with an appropriately qualified clinician. title: UK vs Europe Treatment Methodology
description: How Shift compares UK and overseas bariatric surgery without ranking countries by stereotype or treating a package price as the total cost of care.
keywords: Methodology How we compare UK and overseas bariatric treatment. We do not give countries a “safety score” Excellent and poor providers can exist in the same country. The meaningful unit of comparison is the specific surgeon, hospital, procedure, governance, aftercare and complication pathway. Why these destinations are included Türkiye and parts of Central/Eastern Europe are commonly considered by UK patients seeking self-funded bariatric surgery. Inclusion is not endorsement. True cost The calculator uses user-entered values rather than publishing a stale national “average”. Headline procedure price is separated from flights, companion travel, hotels, specialist insurance, pre-op costs, aftercare, supplements, local transport, lost earnings and a return-trip reserve. GHIC / EHIC UK government guidance states that EHIC/GHIC does not cover travelling abroad for elective surgery or planned treatment. Cards are not substitutes for travel insurance and do not cover private healthcare or repatriation. Follow-up standard BOMSS guidance describes regular postoperative follow-up for a minimum of two years in a specialist bariatric surgical service, followed by at least annual monitoring of nutritional status and supplementation according to need. Why NHS emergency care is not counted as “aftercare included” The NHS may treat emergency complications after someone returns to the UK. That does not turn the NHS into the routine follow-up service that should have been arranged by a privately funded pathway. Country verification sources Where possible, the centre links to government or national regulatory registers: Turkish Ministry of Health authorised international-health-tourism providers; Lithuanian State Health Care Accreditation Agency; Latvian Health Inspectorate; Polish healthcare-provider registers; and Czech national/provider systems. Package completeness score The score only measures how many due-diligence questions the user says they have resolved. It is not a quality score, safety probability, endorsement or clinical recommendation. Medical tourism should be compared as healthcare, not as a holiday package. Flights and hotels are logistics. The product you are actually buying is an operation plus years of clinical consequences and follow-up. Return to UK vs Europe Centre

title: Medication Comparison Centre 2.0
description: Compare UK weight-loss medications side by side: Mounjaro, Wegovy injection, Wegovy tablets, liraglutide/Saxenda and Orlistat, with evidence, administration, NHS context, trade-offs and direct X-vs-Y comparison.
keywords: Home / Knowledge Centre / Compare the treatment — not the hype. Medication Comparison Centre 2.0 Compare the treatment — not the hype. Written and researched by Matt O’Brien, founder of Shift Some Timber. Mounjaro, injectable Wegovy, the new oral Wegovy formulation, liraglutide and Orlistat compared across efficacy evidence, convenience, NHS context, maturity, side-effect burden and maintenance implications. Updated 8 August 2026UK licensed optionsX vs Y battleEvidence-led 2026 matters here. Wegovy is no longer just the familiar 2.4 mg weekly injection story. UK product information now includes a 7.2 mg weekly injectable maintenance option for adults with obesity if needed, and a once-daily 25 mg tablet formulation. Comparisons that ignore those changes are already dated. The current comparison at a glance OptionHow takenRelative efficacyEvidence maturityNHS contextUseful trial anchor Mounjarotirzepatide Weekly injection Very high Very strong NICE-recommended; NHS access is phased / pathway-dependent Up to ~20%+ mean loss in obesity trials; direct head-to-head 20.2% at 72 weeks vs 13.7% semaglutide 1.7/2.4 mg in SURMOUNT-5 Wegovy injectionsemaglutide Weekly injection High Very strong NICE-recommended in specialist weight-management pathways; access depends on pathway STEP 1: mean -14.9% at 68 weeks with 2.4 mg; 7.2 mg is now a licensed maintenance option for adults with obesity if needed Wegovy tabletssemaglutide Daily tablet High Strong but newer formulation Licensed; NICE/NHS positioning may lag the new formulation and should be checked live OASIS 4: mean -13.6% at 64 weeks under treatment-policy analysis; -16.6% estimated while on treatment without additional obesity therapy Liraglutide (Saxenda / licensed equivalents)liraglutide Daily injection Moderate Mature NICE option in specialist services for defined groups; pathway availability varies Large adult trial: mean -8.0% at 56 weeks vs -2.6% placebo Orlistatorlistat Capsule with meals Modest Very mature Long-established NHS option; prescribing criteria and local practice apply Typically produces more modest average loss than GLP-1/GIP medicines; individual response varies Treatment Battle Pick any two licensed options Treatment A Treatment BCompare VS What the evidence actually tells us Mounjaro vs injectable Wegovy SURMOUNT-5 provides a genuine head-to-head anchor: tirzepatide produced greater mean weight loss than semaglutide 1.7/2.4 mg at 72 weeks. That trial does not answer tirzepatide versus the newly licensed 7.2 mg Wegovy dose. Oral Wegovy OASIS 4 gives direct phase 3b evidence for oral semaglutide 25 mg: mean weight change was -13.6% at 64 weeks under the treatment-policy analysis. Liraglutide Saxenda has a mature obesity evidence base, but average loss is lower than the newer weekly incretin options and it requires daily injections. title: Matt’s Story: Why I Built SHIFT
description: The health problems, grief and fright behind Matt’s decision to get help — and why he built SHIFT for support through the ordinary, difficult middle.
keywords: Our story Built by an ordinary bloke, for ordinary blokes. Shift Some Timber started with one fairly simple idea: men's health support should feel useful, honest and human. WHY SHIFT EXISTS Built from lived experience. Kept useful by principle. Shift exists because ordinary blokes deserve better than shame, theatre and miracle marketing. The storyWhy Matt built the thing he wished had existed when he needed it.Explore →The Shift PromiseUseful first, evidence before hype and no judgement.Explore →How we workEditorial standards, governance and the rules behind our recommendations.Explore → I'm Matt. I lost around four and a half stone over about eleven months. But the number only tells you part of the story. The rest is why I needed to change things — and why I built SHIFT. It wasn't just my weight. My knee was in agony, my blood pressure was high, I was taking a pile of tablets, and my clothes looked like I'd been sewn into them. Even ordinary things took planning. Stairs could change how I arranged my day. I was grumpy, moody and drinking to get blackout drunk. I'd also lost grandparents who meant a lot to me. Pain, drinking, grief and how I felt about myself were tangled together. A number on the scales couldn't explain all of that. The fright that helped me take it seriously. Then there were the choking episodes. They happened more than once, sometimes badly enough that we needed an ambulance. I couldn't properly explain what was happening, and I'm not convinced they were connected to my weight. But they frightened me, and added to the serious kick up the arse I needed to do something about my health. I still occasionally wake with a brief episode. Losing weight hasn't made every problem disappear, and I won't pretend it has. The people in my life were a massive part of why I started looking after myself. You don't need a bereavement or a scare to qualify, though. Wanting your evenings back, or wanting ordinary things to feel easier, is reason enough. Giving my head a wobble meant getting help. I changed how I ate, started moving more and used prescribed weight-loss treatment after a clinical assessment. Over about eleven months, I lost around 4½ stone. That's my experience, not a promise about yours. Treatment isn't right for everyone. Whether a medicine is suitable, and what happens during treatment, belongs in a conversation with a qualified prescriber. Getting help mattered. So did the food, movement and ordinary decisions around it. I wasn't becoming a different bloke overnight. I was starting to look after the one who was already there. The changes you can live in. My Next jeans went from a 38/40 to a 32. Adidas went from XXL to L. Those are some of my own markers — clothes I can actually feel comfortable in. I wear Pretty Green and Adidas like I'm sponsored by them. Sadly, both still insist I pay. I had also been under a consultant for sleep apnoea and serious snoring. I'm no longer noticing those problems, but that isn't the same as a consultant confirming the condition has gone. I've cut down my drinking too. I still enjoy a Carling or Guinness with mates; I no longer drink to blackout. That is my account of what changed, not a treatment plan for somebody else. The weight mattered, but so did my knee, my sleep, my mood and how I was living. They all belonged in the same conversation. Why I built SHIFT. Beginning gets plenty of attention. The middle gets less. You've made some changes, then work moves, money gets tight, the knee complains or the people who were meant to help stop answering. You need a way to pick up the plan without rebuilding it from memory. That's where I want SHIFT to earn its place: understand the week you're in, choose a next step that fits, and come back to find out whether it helped. That applies when motivation drops, when life gets messy, when treatment changes and when a clinic goes quiet. Your goals and the practical things you've learned still belong to you. Somewhere to keep the thread. My Timber is free to use in your web browser. You can keep your reason for starting, record what you're trying, choose a Next Shift and return to the answer: did it help? Grub and Fit are the practical food and movement parts of SHIFT. Life Back keeps the reason for doing any of it in view: joining in, feeling more capable or enjoying the ordinary bits of a day. You don't need to buy medicine to use the core check-in. You can also use a notebook, the book's pages or your own notes. What matters is having something useful to come back to. Clear about the limits: A digital record doesn't mean someone is watching over it. My Timber isn't a clinical record, a prescribing service or an emergency line. Medicine questions and symptoms need the appropriate healthcare professional. If a clinic has stopped replying, this guide helps you organise the next steps. SHIFT is a business and may earn money from optional products or partner services. You should be told what costs money, who provides it and who is responsible for clinical decisions. Read our privacy information before recording health details. From one ordinary bloke to another. I haven't built this because I've got every answer. title: Men’s Weight Management FAQs
description: Detailed answers to common questions about men's weight management, GLP-1 treatment, nutrition, activity and health.
keywords: FAQs Proper answers to the questions blokes actually ask. Written and researched by Matt O’Brien, founder of Shift Some Timber. Each question opens into a detailed answer with context, practical next steps and clear medical boundaries. Can men take Mounjaro? Yes, men can be prescribed tirzepatide (Mounjaro) when it is clinically appropriate and they meet the relevant prescribing criteria.Read the detailed answer → Can men take Wegovy? Yes. Wegovy (semaglutide) can be prescribed to eligible adult men following appropriate clinical assessment.Read the detailed answer → Is GLP-1 treatment only for women? No. GLP-1 and related prescription weight-management medicines are not women's treatments.Read the detailed answer → How quickly should a man lose weight? There is no single perfect weekly rate for every man. A sustainable rate depends on starting weight, health, food intake, activity and treatment.Read the detailed answer → Why do men get belly fat? Men commonly store a greater proportion of fat centrally. Genetics, age, hormones, energy balance, activity, sleep and alcohol can all contribute.Read the detailed answer → Does belly fat increase health risk? Higher levels of central or visceral fat are associated with increased cardiometabolic risk.Read the detailed answer → Is BMI accurate for men? BMI is a useful screening measure, but it does not distinguish muscle from fat and does not directly show where body fat is stored.Read the detailed answer → What is a healthy waist-to-height ratio? NHS guidance uses the simple message of trying to keep your waist below half your height.Read the detailed answer → Can walking help weight loss? Yes. Walking increases activity and energy expenditure and can be a sustainable part of weight management.Read the detailed answer → Do I need a gym to lose weight? No. Walking, home exercise, sport, cycling and ordinary daily movement can all contribute.Read the detailed answer → How much protein do men need? Protein needs vary with body size, age, health, activity and goals. A calculator is only a planning estimate.Read the detailed answer → Does sleep affect weight? Yes. Sleep can influence appetite, food choices, energy, mood and activity.Read the detailed answer → Can stress make me gain weight? Stress can contribute indirectly by affecting eating, alcohol, sleep and activity.Read the detailed answer → Does alcohol cause belly fat? Alcohol provides calories and can influence appetite, food choices and sleep.Read the detailed answer → Can I drink alcohol on GLP-1 medication? There is no one answer for everybody. Alcohol may worsen dehydration or gastrointestinal symptoms for some people, so discuss your situation with your prescriber.Read the detailed answer → Can I exercise on GLP-1 treatment? Many people can remain active, but exercise should match health, fitness and treatment effects.Read the detailed answer → Will GLP-1 treatment make me lose muscle? Weight loss can include some lean tissue. Adequate nutrition and resistance exercise can help support muscle and strength.Read the detailed answer → What happens if I stop GLP-1 treatment? Appetite and weight may change after stopping treatment, so maintenance planning and follow-up matter.Read the detailed answer → Is Mounjaro the same as Ozempic? No. Mounjaro contains tirzepatide; Ozempic contains semaglutide.Read the detailed answer → Is Wegovy the same as Ozempic? They both contain semaglutide, but they are distinct branded products with different licensed uses and dosing pathways.Read the detailed answer → Can weight loss lower blood pressure? For many people carrying excess weight, weight loss can contribute to lower blood pressure alongside other measures.Read the detailed answer → Can weight loss improve cholesterol? Weight management, diet and activity can improve parts of the lipid profile for some people.Read the detailed answer → Can losing weight reduce diabetes risk? For people at increased risk of type 2 diabetes, weight loss and lifestyle change can reduce risk.Read the detailed answer → Can weight affect sleep apnoea? Yes. Excess weight is an important risk factor for obstructive sleep apnoea, although it is not the only cause.Read the detailed answer → Why do my knees hurt more after gaining weight? Greater body mass can increase load through weight-bearing joints, but knee pain can have several causes.Read the detailed answer → Does losing weight raise testosterone? Weight loss may improve testosterone levels in some men living with obesity, but symptoms alone cannot diagnose testosterone deficiency.Read the detailed answer → Should men count calories? Calorie tracking can be useful for some men, but it is not compulsory.Read the detailed answer → Are carbs bad for weight loss? No. Carbohydrate is not automatically fattening. Overall energy intake, food quality and portions matter.Read the detailed answer → Is fat bad for weight loss? No. Dietary fat is essential but energy dense, so portions and the wider diet matter.Read the detailed answer → Do I need breakfast to lose weight? No. The best eating pattern is one that supports good nutrition and can be maintained.Read the detailed answer → Can I eat takeaways and still lose weight? Yes. Takeaways can fit into a weight-management plan depending on frequency, portions, sides and drinks.Read the detailed answer → Can I have a BBQ while losing weight? Absolutely. A barbecue can fit into a healthy week.Read the detailed answer → How often should I weigh myself? There is no single right frequency. The useful part is looking at the trend rather than reacting to one reading.Read the detailed answer → Why does my weight change day to day? Water, salt, carbohydrate intake, bowel contents, exercise, alcohol and timing can all move scale weight.Read the detailed answer → What is a weight-loss plateau? A plateau is a period when body weight changes very little despite continued efforts.Read the detailed answer → Is 20% weight loss realistic for everyone? No. A 20% reduction is a major milestone, not a universal target.Read the detailed answer → What is the 20% Club? A milestone some people use to describe losing 20% of their starting body weight. It is not a universal target.Read the detailed answer → What is The Timber Mill? The Shift Some Timber shop for clothing, useful gear, guides and future member rewards.Read the detailed answer → What is a Founding Shifter? Someone who joins Shift and wants useful updates.Read the detailed answer → Is the Health MOT a medical assessment? No. It is an informational self-check and does not diagnose a condition or establish treatment eligibility.Read the detailed answer → Does Shift Some Timber prescribe medication yet? No. Shift Some Timber does not prescribe or supply medication.Read the detailed answer → Will my Health MOT data be saved? Public Health MOT answers are not saved to a member health history unless you use an account-backed feature that clearly tells you it will save them.Read the detailed answer → Can women use the public tools? The public calculators are general information tools, although the brand voice is designed around adult men.Read the detailed answer → Is Shift Some Timber a replacement for my GP? No. It is not a replacement for NHS primary care, emergency services or individual medical assessment.Read the detailed answer → Sources & evidence Check the underlying guidance directly: MHRA — GLP-1 medicines: what you need to know NICE — Overweight and obesity management (NG246)

No overall winner We do not assign numerical treatment scores or calculate an overall winner. Different people value different dimensions, and some clinical considerations cannot be reduced to preference at all. Normalisation We do not map treatments, access routes and countries onto a shared numerical scale. A location or funding route does not itself cause weight loss; compare the actual treatment and care pathway. Personalisation Use your priorities to prepare questions about costs, treatment burden, reversibility and follow-up. The comparison does not select a preferred treatment from a saved profile. Source inheritance The universal centre inherits the evidence and caveats documented in the Medication, Surgery, Lifestyle, NHS vs Private and UK vs Europe methodology pages. title: Lifestyle vs Treatment Centre
description: Compare lifestyle-only weight loss with medication, bariatric surgery and combined treatment, plus structured programmes, walking, cardio and strength training.
keywords: Home / Knowledge Centre / Should you try doing it yourself first? Lifestyle vs Treatment Centre Should you try doing it yourself first? Written and researched by Matt O’Brien, founder of Shift Some Timber. Compare structured lifestyle support with medication and surgery — then drill into walking, strength, DIY dieting and combined-treatment approaches. Updated 8 August 2026Lifestyle vs medicationLifestyle vs surgeryX vs Y engine The false choice: Medication and surgery are not alternatives to lifestyle. NICE says medicines for weight management should be used alongside a reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity. Lifestyle is the foundation; the real question is whether additional biological or procedural support is warranted. Routes at a glance ApproachWeight-loss potentialSpeedMedical intensityAppetite supportMaintenance Structured lifestyle Shift Programme Moderate on average, highly variable Gradual Low Does not directly pharmacologically suppress appetite Skills can be maintained indefinitely; relapse plan still needed Lifestyle + weight-loss medication High for effective modern medicines; varies by drug Usually faster than lifestyle alone Prescription treatment / monitoring Can directly reduce hunger/appetite/food noise depending on medicine Long-term medicine and/or structured maintenance often required Lifestyle + bariatric surgery Very high for established major bariatric procedures Often rapid early loss Highest treatment intensity Procedure-dependent effects on restriction, gut hormones and appetite Lifelong nutrition, supplements and follow-up may be required DIY dieting Variable Variable Low No direct pharmacological support Depends entirely on plan quality and sustainability Lifestyle Battle Compare any two approaches Approach A Approach BCompare VS When lifestyle-first makes particular sense You have not actually tried a structured plan A defined calorie/meal structure, adequate protein, regular walking and two strength sessions is very different from repeatedly “being good” for four days. You prefer minimal medical treatment For someone who strongly wants to avoid medication/procedures, a time-limited structured lifestyle trial with an agreed review point can be reasonable. Your health risk is lower Where obesity-related disease and treatment urgency are lower, there may be more room to test lifestyle changes before escalating treatment discussions. When additional treatment becomes more worth discussing Repeated regain If meaningful losses repeatedly return despite genuine effort, repeating the identical plan harder may not be the smartest next experiment. High hunger or food noise Behaviour matters, but appetite biology matters too. Medication may make the lifestyle component easier to execute for some people. Higher health risk Severe obesity or important weight-related disease can make delaying evidence-based medical or surgical discussion less attractive. Exercise: what actually belongs in the plan? UK guidance recommends adults work toward at least of moderate-intensity activity a week or equivalent, plus strengthening activity for major muscle groups on at least 2 days a week. Walking can contribute to the aerobic target; it does not replace strength work. title: Orlistat: a practical UK guide
description: Orlistat is a weight-management capsule that reduces absorption of some of the fat in food. The practical question is whether its benefits, bowel side effects and meal routine suit you—not whether a capsule sounds easier than an injection.
keywords: Orlistat: a practical UK guide Prepared by the Shift Some Timber Editorial Team. Sources checked 3 October 2026; this is not independent clinical review. Orlistat is a weight-management capsule that reduces absorption of some of the fat in food. The practical question is whether its benefits, bowel side effects and meal routine suit you—not whether a capsule sounds easier than an injection. Which product are we talking about? This guide concerns prescription orlistat 120 mg. Lower-dose orlistat 60 mg is a separate pharmacy medicine, with its own eligibility checks and instructions. Do not swap doses or assume that all orlistat is prescription-only. Who can be considered? The Xenical 120 mg licence covers BMI of at least 30, or at least 28 with associated risk factors, alongside a reduced-calorie diet. Meeting a BMI threshold does not establish individual suitability. A prescriber or pharmacist needs your medical history and current medicines. What does taking it involve? The product information links doses to main meals containing fat. A missed meal or a meal without fat means omitting that dose. Use the instructions supplied with your own prescription. More capsules are not a way to cancel out a large meal. Side effects and other medicines Oily stools, wind with discharge and urgent bowel movements can occur, particularly with higher-fat meals. Tell the clinician about bowel, liver or kidney conditions and all medicines, including warfarin, ciclosporin, thyroid or epilepsy treatment. Ask whether vitamin supplementation or additional monitoring is needed. Persistent or severe symptoms need medical advice. How will you know whether it is worth continuing? The 120 mg product information sets a review point: stop treatment if at least 5% of starting body weight has not been lost after 12 weeks. Arrange that review with your prescriber rather than repeatedly buying without checking benefit and tolerability. Questions before paying Which strength and brand are you supplying, and what is included in the price? Who checks my other medicines and answers a side-effect question? When is my progress review, and what happens if treatment is not helping? What would a realistic meal pattern look like around my working day? Make the routine workable Write down your usual meals before the consultation. Be honest about takeaway nights, shift work and days when you skip lunch. The aim is a plan you can actually follow. In My Timber, you can save meals, choose manageable movement and check in on progress whether or not you buy treatment through SHIFT. Medicine decisions stay with your prescriber. Sources and further reading Xenical 120 mg: UK product information MHRA: prescription and pharmacy orlistat About this guide General information for adults, not a prescription or an individual assessment. Product information and your own clinician’s instructions take priority. This update replaces an incomplete guide with medicine-specific information and direct sources. title: Lifestyle vs Treatment Methodology
description: How Shift compares lifestyle intervention, weight-loss medication, bariatric surgery, walking and strength without pretending they are mutually exclusive alternatives.
keywords: Methodology How we compare lifestyle with medical treatment. Written and researched by Matt O’Brien, founder of Shift Some Timber. They are not mutually exclusive NICE NG246 says medicines for weight management should be used alongside a reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity. Bariatric pathways also include dietary, behavioural and follow-up care. Our comparison therefore treats lifestyle as a foundation rather than a competing brand. Why lifestyle gets a lower weight-loss rating Behavioural programmes can produce clinically meaningful loss, but average losses are generally lower than modern effective anti-obesity medicines or major bariatric surgery. That does not make lifestyle unimportant; it means weight-loss intensity and health-behaviour value are different dimensions. Why strength scores highly for muscle but not scale loss Resistance training is important for strength, function and lean-mass preservation. It is not primarily a rapid scale-weight intervention. Physical activity benchmark NHS guidance recommends at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity activity per week or 75 minutes of vigorous-intensity activity, plus strengthening activity on at least 2 days per week for adults. Ratings are not probabilities The 0–10 comparison values are editorial decision aids. A 10/10 appetite-support rating does not mean everybody experiences complete appetite suppression. When we escalate language The Treatment Finder can personalise context using reported repeated regain, hunger, food noise, cost sensitivity and preference for medical intervention. It still does not prescribe. Lifestyle should not be weaponised. “Lifestyle matters” does not mean someone must repeatedly fail unsupported diets before being allowed to discuss evidence-based treatment. Return to Lifestyle vs Treatment Health information General information, not individual medical advice. Where treatment suitability matters, the decision belongs with an appropriately qualified clinician. title: Saxenda (liraglutide): a practical UK guide
description: Saxenda is a daily prescription injection for weight management. Understanding the daily routine, side effects and review point matters more than treating it as an older version of a weekly jab.
keywords: Saxenda (liraglutide): a practical UK guide Prepared by the Shift Some Timber Editorial Team. Sources checked 3 October 2026; this is not independent clinical review. Saxenda is a daily prescription injection for weight management. Understanding the daily routine, side effects and review point matters more than treating it as an older version of a weekly jab. What is Saxenda? Saxenda contains liraglutide, a GLP-1 receptor agonist. It is used with reduced-calorie eating and increased physical activity. It is injected daily, unlike weekly products. This page covers adults; it does not assess suitability for a child or teenager. Who can be considered? The adult licence covers BMI of at least 30, or BMI from 27 to below 30 with a weight-related condition. The prescriber must assess the whole medical picture. A licence threshold does not guarantee NHS access, private acceptance or available stock. Starting and reviewing treatment The dose is increased gradually under the prescribed schedule. The adult continuation rule is measured after 12 weeks at 3 mg daily: treatment should stop if less than 5% of initial body weight has been lost. That is not simply 12 weeks from the first injection. Agree the review date with your prescriber. Side effects need a plan Nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea and constipation can occur. Persistent severe abdominal pain needs urgent medical assessment because pancreatitis is a recognised risk. Seek advice if vomiting prevents adequate drinking. Tell the prescriber about other medicines, especially diabetes treatment; do not change insulin yourself. Read the leaflet for the full warnings. Questions that make a comparison useful Can I manage a daily injection and the storage instructions around work or travel? Who will advise me if a dose increase is difficult? What do I do if supply is interrupted or I miss several days? What is the cost at my prescribed maintenance dose, including reviews and supplies? If this does not help enough, who reviews the alternatives? Do not improvise a switch Ask the prescriber for written instructions if changing medicine or restarting after a gap. Products are not interchangeable simply because they belong to the same family. Do not combine treatments or copy another person's schedule. Keep support after the prescription Before starting, decide where practical food and movement help will come from and who answers treatment questions. Keep those routes somewhere easy to find. My Timber offers everyday planning and check-ins without a treatment purchase; it does not prescribe, change doses or monitor clinical safety. Sources and further reading Saxenda: UK product information MHRA: GLP-1 medicines for weight loss and diabetes About this guide General information for adults, not a prescription or an individual assessment. Product information and your own clinician’s instructions take priority. This update replaces an incomplete guide with medicine-specific information and direct sources. title: Progress Centre Methodology & Privacy
description: How the Shift Progress Centre stores and interprets weight, waist, BMI, blood pressure, steps, sleep and treatment-tracking data.
keywords: Home / Tools / How the Progress Centre works. Transparency How the Progress Centre works. Written and researched by Matt O’Brien, founder of Shift Some Timber. The dashboard is designed to show trends and organise information. It is not remote medical monitoring. Where your data is stored The static Progress Centre uses browser localStorage on the device you are using. In this release, your entries are not synced to a server or account. Clearing browser storage can delete them, so use the export function if you want a backup. What it calculates BMI is recalculated from your Health MOT height and each saved weight. Weight and waist charts show the values you enter over time. The dashboard does not estimate body-fat percentage or predict medical outcomes. Blood pressure Blood pressure can be logged for trend purposes, but the dashboard does not diagnose hypertension. NHS interpretation depends on how and where readings are taken and on repeated measurements. Steps, sleep, protein and hydration These are self-reported progress measures. They are useful for spotting patterns but do not prove causation. A low-weight-loss week with better sleep and activity can still be a useful week. Treatment tracker The tracker stores treatment name, dose/stage, start date and a broad side-effect status. It does not recommend dose changes, tell you when to titrate or replace prescriber review. Maintenance range A personal maintenance range is a behavioural tool, not a clinical standard. The dashboard deliberately avoids declaring a single “correct” maintenance weight. Data keys used sstHealthProfile sstHealthMotPriorities sstProgressEntries sstTreatmentProgress sstMaintenancePlan What this release does not do It does not send emergency alerts, diagnose high blood pressure, interpret blood tests, provide clinical dose advice or guarantee that local browser data will persist forever. title: Surgery Comparison Methodology
description: How Shift compares bariatric procedures across weight loss, reflux, diabetes, nutritional burden, recovery, reversibility, revision and NHS context.
keywords: Methodology How we compare bariatric procedures. Written and researched by Matt O’Brien, founder of Shift Some Timber. We compare trade-offs, not just the biggest weight-loss number. Weight-loss evidence Different studies report total weight loss, excess weight loss or BMI change. We avoid pretending those measures are interchangeable. We present the evidence without numerical treatment ratings or a pooled personal forecast. Reflux Reflux can materially alter procedure choice. Sleeve may worsen reflux in some people, while Roux-en-Y bypass can be attractive in selected patients with significant reflux. No website can replace endoscopy/history/surgeon assessment. Diabetes and metabolic effect Bypass procedures have extensive metabolic-surgery evidence. That does not mean every person with diabetes should have a bypass. Nutritional burden All bariatric procedures require long-term follow-up. Bypass procedures generally carry greater risk of micronutrient deficiency and malabsorption; band, balloon and ESG avoid intestinal bypass but still require good nutrition and clinical follow-up. Reversibility “Reversible” is used cautiously. Bands and balloons can be removed. ESG can sometimes be revised. Bypass can be surgically revised. None of that means the body simply returns to exactly its previous state without consequence. NHS relevance This reflects how established the procedure is within UK bariatric pathways, not a promise that a local NHS service offers it. NICE referral criteria NICE NG246 recommends referral for comprehensive bariatric assessment at BMI 40+, or BMI 35–39.9 with a significant weight-related condition that could improve with weight loss, subject to the complete guideline and ethnicity-adjusted thresholds where relevant. Endoscopic procedures The NHS now describes ESG in its weight-loss procedure information. ESG and balloon are included because users compare them with surgery, but their invasiveness, durability and evidence are different. No hidden “best surgery” score. The strongest procedure for weight loss may not be the strongest choice for reflux, nutritional simplicity, reversibility or personal preference. title: Health MOT Methodology & Limitations
description: How the Shift Health MOT interprets BMI, waist-to-height ratio, blood pressure, sleep, activity and behaviour — and what it deliberately does not diagnose.
keywords: Home / Tools / How the Shift Health MOT works. Transparency How the Shift Health MOT works. Written and researched by Matt O’Brien, founder of Shift Some Timber. The Health MOT is designed to organise information and priorities, not manufacture a clinical diagnosis from a questionnaire. Why there is no overall health score A single 0–100 score would imply a level of validated clinical precision this tool does not have. Instead, the MOT separates different domains and labels them Good foundation, Worth reviewing, or Higher priority. BMI and waist Adult BMI uses weight kg ÷ height metres². NICE classifies standard adult overweight at BMI 25–29.9 and obesity from 30, with lower BMI thresholds used for several ethnic groups because cardiometabolic risk occurs at lower BMI. Waist-to-height ratio is used as additional central-adiposity context, particularly when BMI is below 35. Blood pressure NHS guidance usually considers blood pressure high at 140/90 mmHg or above in a healthcare setting, or 135/85 or above for home readings. A single reading does not diagnose hypertension. Very high readings require proper clinical interpretation, especially if symptoms are present. Sleep apnoea signal The MOT flags reported breathing pauses, gasping/choking, loud snoring and significant daytime sleepiness because these are NHS-listed symptoms of sleep apnoea. It does not calculate an apnoea score or diagnose the condition. Physical activity Current UK guidance recommends adults work toward at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity activity a week (or equivalent vigorous activity) plus strengthening activity on at least 2 days. The MOT treats lower activity as an opportunity to build capacity, not as a failure. Alcohol The UK low-risk drinking guideline is no more than 14 units per week on a regular basis, spread across 3 or more days if drinking that amount. Nutrition, stress and emotional eating These sections use behavioural prompts rather than validated diagnostic scales. Regular loss-of-control eating is escalated because binge-eating disorder is a recognised condition that deserves appropriate assessment rather than stricter dieting. Weight-loss scenarios The 5%, 10%, 15%, 20% and 25% table performs simple arithmetic on current weight and BMI. It deliberately does not predict a precise blood-pressure reduction, diabetes remission probability or other individual medical outcome. Local storage and privacy The legacy browser Health MOT questionnaire stores its answers and report data in local storage on the device where it runs. It does not upload them to SHIFT or into My Timber. A shared browser can retain sensitive answers after the page closes. Clear this site’s browser data to remove the local copy; that does not erase separate account-backed information. The main Health MOT link now leads to the separate SHIFT Health home blood-test information page. This methodology describes the older questionnaire, not a laboratory service or enabled results integration. Sources NICE NG246 – identifying overweight, obesity and central adiposity NHS – blood pressure test NHS – sleep apnoea NHS – physical activity guidelines NHS – alcohol units and guidance What this tool will never do It will not diagnose diabetes, hypertension, sleep apnoea, an eating disorder or cardiovascular disease. It will not prescribe Mounjaro, Wegovy or surgery. Those decisions require appropriate clinical assessment. Take the Health MOT Health information General information, not individual medical advice. Where treatment suitability matters, the decision belongs with an appropriately qualified clinician.

title: NHS vs Private Methodology
description: How Shift compares NHS and private weight-management access without confusing NICE eligibility, commissioning, waiting times, provider regulation and price.
keywords: Methodology How we compare NHS and private treatment. Written and researched by Matt O’Brien, founder of Shift Some Timber. NICE criteria vs NHS access We deliberately separate a NICE recommendation from real-world access. NHS England's current tirzepatide implementation uses phased primary-care cohorts and local ICB delivery models, while specialist weight-management services use the broader NICE-eligible cohort subject to prescribing approval and resource prioritisation. England vs the UK NHS England guidance is not a universal description of Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland. Where a route depends on commissioning or prescription charges, this site labels the England-specific context rather than pretending one answer applies nationally. Private does not mean unregulated Private medicines remain prescription-only and need proper clinical assessment. NHS England's 2026 commissioning guidance cites updated GPhC guidance: high-risk weight-management prescribing should not rely solely on an online questionnaire and relevant information should be independently verified. Why we do not hard-code private prices Provider prices change by medicine, dose, consultation model and time. The calculator therefore uses the user's actual quoted monthly, setup and recurring-extra costs rather than publishing stale “typical” prices. Cost score The lower-cost rating reflects direct treatment fees, not the value of someone's time, travel, lost earnings or health cost of waiting. Those are individual factors and should not be disguised as objective pounds. Speed score Private care generally scores higher for potential speed, but this is not a waiting-time guarantee. NHS and private capacity both vary. Quality We do not assume NHS care is automatically high quality or private care automatically superior. The framework compares monitoring, continuity, support, record integration and access. Access is part of treatment. A theoretically perfect medicine or operation is not useful if the route is inaccessible, unaffordable, unsafe or impossible to maintain. keywords: Review policy How We Review Products Commercial relationships are disclosed. The verdict still belongs to us. Editorial independence We may receive products free of charge, earn affiliate commission or work with a brand commercially. None of those arrangements automatically determines what we say about a product. What we consider Is it useful for the audience? Does it work for its intended everyday purpose? Does the price represent reasonable value? Are health or performance claims proportionate and supportable? Is there a cheaper or simpler option that does the same job? title: The Blood Pressure Guide for Men
description: A blood pressure reading is useful when you know how it was taken, what the two numbers mean and who will review it. Use this guide to prepare for that conversation, rather than trying to diagnose or treat yourself from one reading.
keywords: Home / The Blood Pressure Guide for Men Cornerstone guide The Blood Pressure Guide for Men A blood pressure reading is useful when you know how it was taken, what the two numbers mean and who will review it. Use this guide to prepare for that conversation, rather than trying to diagnose or treat yourself from one reading. Know what you are looking at The first number describes pressure as the heart pumps; the second describes pressure between beats. Keep both numbers and the measurement date. A useful note might say where you were measured, whether you had rested and whether this was an isolated reading or part of a series. A cropped screenshot without that context is harder to interpret. Clinic and home thresholds differ The NHS describes high blood pressure as usually 140/90 mmHg or above when measured by a healthcare professional, or 135/85 mmHg or above at home. These are assessment thresholds, not instructions to start or change medicines. Repeat or ambulatory measurements may be needed. Your clinician sets any personal treatment target. Make the next check easier Ask your pharmacist or practice whether you need a repeat check, a home series or a 24-hour monitor. If home monitoring is recommended, ask which monitor and cuff size are suitable and how to use them. Take the complete readings and your current medicine list to the review. Include missed doses honestly. Agree when the results will be reviewed and whom to contact if you are concerned before then. Choose a practical habit alongside clinical care Pick one part of your usual week to improve: compare salt on two foods you often buy, plan a short walk you can repeat, or look honestly at the drinks you have most evenings. Choose something measurable and affordable. Lifestyle changes can help, but feeling fitter or losing weight does not prove your blood pressure is controlled. Do not wait for a calculator if you are unwell Sudden persistent chest pain, especially with pain spreading or sweating, sickness or breathlessness, needs emergency help through 999. The NHS advises 111 for other concerning symptoms such as recurring headaches, blurred vision or chest pain that comes and goes. Do not use this page or the Health MOT to decide that serious symptoms are safe. Keep the medicine decision with your clinician Record the name and dose you actually take, any difficulties taking it and questions about side effects. Do not stop or adjust prescribed treatment because one reading looks better. At the appointment, ask: what do my readings show, what is the next action, and when do we check again? Leave with those three answers rather than another unexplained number. Sources and further reading NHS — high blood pressure, thresholds and urgent advice NHS — blood pressure testing Your next step Read the weight and blood pressure guide → Shift Says Use this page as information, not judgement. The best next step is the one that actually fits your health, your life and what you are ready to change. Can I do this myself? Absolutely. You do not have to join a paid Shift Programme to start improving your health. Use our free Knowledge Hub, calculators, Health MOT and tools to have a proper go first. title: Gastric Band UK: The Definitive Decision Guide
description: A comprehensive UK guide to adjustable gastric band surgery: how it works, band fills, weight loss, slippage, erosion, long-term follow-up.
keywords: Home / Treatment Centre / Surgery / Gastric Band UK: The Definitive Decision Guide Surgery Decision Guide Gastric Band UK: The Definitive Decision Guide Written and researched by Matt O’Brien, founder of Shift Some Timber. A comprehensive UK guide to adjustable gastric band surgery: how it works, band fills, weight loss, slippage, erosion, long-term follow-up, removal and comparisons with sleeve, ESG and medication. Updated 8 August 2026UK-focusedNHS + private contextEvidence-led Jump to what matters30-second answer →What is a gastric band? →How it works →Band fills & adjustments →Expected weight loss →Who might it suit? →Why popularity declined →NHS availability →Private route →Eating with a band →Risks & complications →Band slippage →Erosion & port problems →Pregnancy →Weight regain →Removal & revision →Band vs sleeve →Band vs medication →Questions to ask →Shift Says →Printable checklist →FAQs →Sources → The 30-second answer An adjustable gastric band is a silicone ring placed around the upper stomach. It creates a small upper pouch and a narrow opening into the rest of the stomach. A port under the skin allows the band to be tightened or loosened with fluid. It does not remove stomach or bypass intestine. That makes it adjustable and removable — but it also usually produces slower, more modest weight loss than sleeve or bypass and requires ongoing band management. What exactly is a gastric band? The NHS describes a band placed around the upper part of the stomach, creating a smaller pouch so less food is needed before you feel full. North Bristol NHS describes a silicone tube with an inflatable section connected to a small port beneath the skin. The band is placed laparoscopically under general anaesthetic. Unlike sleeve or bypass surgery, the stomach is not cut away and the intestine is not rerouted. How does it work? Restriction Food passes through a narrower opening, slowing eating and reducing the amount comfortably eaten at one time. Satiety A well-adjusted band can reduce appetite and encourage earlier fullness. Behaviour The band only works properly when meals are slow, small and well-chewed. Liquid calories and grazing can bypass its intended effect. What are band fills? The access port allows a bariatric clinician to add or remove saline from the band. Adding fluid increases restriction; removing fluid loosens it. Adjustments are often spaced over weeks or months and are guided by hunger, satiety, eating tolerance and weight-loss progress. A band that is too tight can cause vomiting, reflux or difficulty swallowing. More restriction is not automatically better. How much weight could I lose? Weight loss after a band is generally slower and less predictable than after sleeve or bypass. NHS and bariatric services often describe outcomes using excess-weight loss rather than total-body-weight loss, which makes headline comparisons tricky. The important point is that the band usually requires active long-term adjustment and very strong eating-behaviour adherence. Some people do very well; others experience inadequate loss or eventually require revision/removal. Who might a band still suit? Someone who strongly values adjustability and the absence of stomach removal. Someone prepared for repeated follow-up and band fills. Someone who understands the eating pattern required and does not rely heavily on liquid calories or grazing. Someone whose bariatric team considers the risk/benefit profile appropriate compared with sleeve, bypass or medication. Why is the gastric band less popular than it used to be? Its appeal was obvious: keyhole surgery, no stomach removal, adjustability and removability. Over time, however, higher reoperation rates, slippage, erosion, port problems and less predictable long-term weight loss led many bariatric programmes to favour sleeve or bypass. That does not make the band “bad”. It means it deserves a more honest discussion than it sometimes received in the early 2000s. Is gastric band still available on the NHS? The NHS still lists gastric banding among the main types of weight-loss surgery, but local bariatric centres differ in what they routinely offer. Many centres now favour sleeve and bypass procedures because of longer-term outcome and revision considerations. What about going private? If considering a private band, ask what follow-up and number of fills are included. A headline operation price can be misleading if future adjustments, imaging, port replacement or removal are extra. You also need to know who manages you if the band becomes too tight or slips years later. What is eating like with a band? Meals need to be small, slow and thoroughly chewed. Tough, dry or fibrous foods can be difficult for some people. Drinking with meals may reduce the intended satiety effect, while high-calorie liquids can pass through the band easily and undermine weight loss. Repeated vomiting is not a normal sign that the band is “working”. It needs review. What can go wrong? Band-specific issues Band slippage Erosion into the stomach Port or tubing problems Over-tightening Reflux / oesophageal symptoms General surgical risks Bleeding Infection Blood clot Anaesthetic complications Need for later revision Band slippage The NHS specifically warns that a gastric band can move out of position. Symptoms can include persistent heartburn, nausea and vomiting. If the band has slipped, further surgery may be needed to reposition or remove it. Persistent vomiting or inability to swallow properly is not something to sit on. Contact your bariatric team or seek urgent medical assessment depending on severity. Band erosion, port and tubing problems Over time, the band can rarely erode into the stomach wall. The access port can rotate, become infected or disconnect from the tubing. These are reasons why a technically “reversible” device can still create years of follow-up and additional procedures. Pregnancy with a gastric band Pregnancy should be discussed with the bariatric team. The band may need adjustment during pregnancy depending on symptoms, nutrition and weight gain. As with other bariatric procedures, pregnancy planning is best done after the rapid weight-loss phase and with nutritional monitoring. Can weight return with a band? Yes. The band does not prevent grazing, liquid calories or gradual behavioural adaptation. Some people also lose restriction over time or simply do not achieve enough satiety to sustain a meaningful deficit. Can the band be removed? Yes, but removal is another operation. After removal, weight regain is common unless another treatment strategy is in place. Some people convert from a band to sleeve or bypass, depending on anatomy, reflux and surgeon assessment. Gastric band vs sleeve BandSleeve Anatomy Device around stomach; no stomach removed 75–80% of stomach removed Adjustable? Yes No Typical long-term effectiveness More variable Generally stronger and more predictable Device issues Possible No implanted band Reflux Can occur Can worsen Band vs modern medication Modern incretin medicines avoid surgery. Studies of medicines and bands involve different participants and follow-up periods, so headline weight-loss figures alone cannot establish which is better for you. A band has no recurring drug cost but can create long-term device and revision costs. The right choice depends on health, preference, eligibility and willingness to engage with follow-up. Questions to ask before choosing a band Why a band rather than sleeve or medication? How many fills are included? What is your band-removal/revision rate? Who manages a slipped band? What happens if I move away? How often is imaging needed? What are your long-term weight-loss outcomes? What will removal cost? Shift Says Our take The band still has a place, but it is no longer the obvious “simple reversible option” it was once sold as. The long-term maintenance burden and revision risk need to be front and centre. If you were our brother, we'd ask why a band is better for you than sleeve, medication or ESG — and we'd want a very convincing answer. Printable band checklist I understand the band requires ongoing adjustments. I know it can slip or erode. I know who manages urgent band problems. I understand weight loss may be slower/more variable. I have compared it with sleeve, medication and ESG. I know the cost of fills, removal and revision.Print / Save FAQs Is a gastric band reversible? It can be removed, but removal requires another operation and does not guarantee reversal of all symptoms or weight change. Can a band slip? Yes. The NHS lists band slippage as a recognised complication. Do I need band fills forever? Many people need periodic adjustments, especially during the first years. Is a band safer than a sleeve? They have different risk profiles. A band avoids stomach removal but creates device-specific long-term risks. Can I regain weight? Yes. Regain can occur through eating pattern, loss of restriction or inadequate satiety. Is the band still used? Yes, although it is less commonly chosen than it once was.
