title: Gastric Balloon UK: The Definitive Decision Guide
description: A comprehensive UK guide to gastric balloons: types, insertion, expected weight loss, nausea, deflation, removal, NHS/private use.
keywords: Home / Treatment Centre / Surgery / Gastric Balloon UK: The Definitive Decision Guide Surgery Decision Guide Gastric Balloon UK: The Definitive Decision Guide Written and researched by Matt O’Brien, founder of Shift Some Timber. A comprehensive UK guide to gastric balloons: types, insertion, expected weight loss, nausea, deflation, removal, NHS/private use, aftercare and comparisons with medication, ESG and surgery. Updated 8 August 2026UK-focusedNHS + private contextEvidence-led Jump to what matters30-second answer →What is a gastric balloon? →Types of balloon →How it works →Expected weight loss →Who might it suit? →NHS use →Private route →Insertion →The first week →Diet with a balloon →How long it stays →Removal / passing naturally →Risks →Deflation & migration →Balloon vs medication →Balloon vs surgery →Balloon vs ESG →After removal →Questions to ask →Shift Says →Printable checklist →FAQs →Sources → The 30-second answer A gastric balloon is a temporary device placed inside the stomach to take up space, increase fullness and help reduce food intake. Most traditional balloons are placed endoscopically and removed after around 6–12 months; swallowable systems are designed to pass naturally after a shorter period. It is less invasive than bariatric surgery, but the trade-off is usually less weight loss and a stronger reliance on maintaining habits after the balloon is gone. What is a gastric balloon? A gastric balloon is a soft balloon that sits in the stomach. Traditional systems are inserted through the mouth using an endoscope and then filled with saline or air. South Tees and Hull NHS information describe it as a short-term tool that reduces hunger and helps people feel full sooner. What kinds of balloon exist? Endoscopic fluid-filled balloon Inserted under endoscopy and removed later by endoscopy. Common examples stay 6 or 12 months depending on device. Swallowable balloon Swallowed as a capsule, filled after imaging confirmation, then designed to empty and pass naturally after several months. Bridge-to-surgery balloon Sometimes used to reduce weight and operative risk before another procedure. How does the balloon work? The balloon occupies space and can slow gastric emptying, helping you feel full sooner. It is not a hormonal medicine and it does not permanently change your anatomy. How much weight could I lose? Results vary by balloon system, treatment length and behavioural support. Chelsea and Westminster NHS says average loss can be up to around 20 kg through balloon treatment combined with diet and activity. Somerset NHS reported average losses around 10–15% of body weight with the Allurion programme after approximately four months. Those figures are from different devices and patient groups, so they should not be treated as interchangeable promises. Who might a balloon suit? Someone wanting a temporary, non-surgical intervention. Someone needing moderate rather than very large weight loss. Someone who cannot or does not want bariatric surgery. Someone using it as a bridge to a safer later operation. Someone willing to use the balloon period to build habits for after removal. Is gastric balloon available on the NHS? Some NHS bariatric services use intragastric balloons, often for selected patients or as a bridge to surgery rather than as a routine long-term obesity treatment for everyone. Availability varies by region and centre. Private gastric balloon treatment Private balloon programmes should include more than insertion. Ask what dietetic support, anti-sickness medication, emergency contact, removal, follow-up and behavioural support are included. What is insertion like? Traditional balloons are usually passed through the mouth using an endoscope. Depending on the device and service, sedation or anaesthesia may be used. The balloon is then filled inside the stomach. Swallowable balloons follow a different pathway and may not require endoscopy for placement or removal. Why can the first few days be rough? Nausea, cramping and vomiting are common as the stomach adjusts to a foreign object. Services often prescribe anti-sickness and acid-suppression medication and use a liquid diet initially. Persistent inability to keep fluids down needs medical review. Dehydration can become serious quickly. Eating with a balloon Diet progresses from fluids to soft food and then small normal meals. The balloon works best when people avoid grazing and calorie-dense liquids and use the provider’s support programme to learn slower eating, portion awareness and better food choices. How long does it stay in? Chelsea and Westminster NHS says balloons can remain in place around 6–12 months depending on the device. Leaving a balloon longer than intended can increase the risk of material deterioration and deflation. How is the balloon removed? Traditional systems are emptied and removed endoscopically. Some swallowable systems are designed to empty through a valve and pass naturally through the digestive tract after several months. What can go wrong? Common Nausea Vomiting Cramping Reflux Abdominal discomfort Less common but important Dehydration Ulceration Balloon deflation Migration / obstruction Need for early removal What happens if a balloon deflates or migrates? A deflated balloon can move out of the stomach. Some devices use coloured fluid so urine colour change can warn of leakage. Migration can rarely lead to bowel obstruction and urgent treatment. Balloon vs weight-loss medication A balloon is temporary and mechanical; medication is systemic and often longer-term. Medication may produce greater or more sustained weight loss for some people, but requires ongoing prescribing and may have recurring cost. Balloon treatment avoids long-term drug exposure but ends when the device leaves. Balloon vs surgery A balloon does not cut or permanently alter anatomy and usually has faster recovery. Sleeve and bypass generally produce larger and more durable average weight loss but carry surgical and lifelong nutritional consequences. Balloon vs ESG ESG uses endoscopic sutures to reduce stomach volume and is intended as a more durable anatomical change than a temporary balloon. It is still less invasive than conventional surgery. What happens after the balloon is gone? This is the real test. Hunger and stomach capacity are no longer mechanically affected by the device, so weight can return if no sustainable habits or follow-up plan exist. The balloon should be treated as a temporary training window, not six months of rented willpower. Questions to ask a balloon provider Which balloon system do you use? How long does it stay? Is removal included? What happens if I cannot tolerate it? Who manages severe vomiting? What weight loss do you see in your own patients? What behavioural support is included? What happens after removal? Shift Says Our take The balloon can be a useful middle ground: more than lifestyle-only, less permanent than surgery. But temporary treatment needs a permanent plan. If follow-up ends the day the balloon comes out, we'd be wary. Printable balloon checklist I know which balloon I am getting. I know how it is inserted and removed. I understand first-week nausea/vomiting risk. I know what support is included. I have a plan for after removal. I have compared balloon with medication and ESG.Print / Save FAQs How long does a gastric balloon stay in? Typically around 6–12 months for traditional systems, depending on device; swallowable balloons may pass after a shorter period. Is a balloon surgery? No. It is an intragastric device and does not involve cutting the stomach. How much weight can I lose? Results vary. NHS sources report figures ranging from about 10–15% body weight in some programmes to average losses up to around 20kg. Will I feel sick? Nausea, cramps and vomiting are common in the first days. Can the balloon burst? Deflation is uncommon but possible; migration can require urgent assessment. Will weight come back? It can, especially if long-term eating/activity habits are not established. title: Weight-Loss Surgery UK: The Definitive Decision Guide
description: Understand bariatric surgery in the UK: sleeve, bypass, band, balloon and ESG, NHS eligibility, private treatment, costs, risks, recovery.
keywords: Home / Treatment Centre / Surgery / Weight-Loss Surgery UK: The Definitive Decision Guide Surgery Decision Guide Weight-Loss Surgery UK: The Definitive Decision Guide Written and researched by Matt O’Brien, founder of Shift Some Timber. Understand bariatric surgery in the UK: sleeve, bypass, band, balloon and ESG, NHS eligibility, private treatment, costs, risks, recovery, lifelong follow-up and how surgery compares with medication. Updated 8 August 2026UK-focusedNHS + privateEvidence-led Jump to what matters30-second answer →What is bariatric surgery? →Compare main surgery types →Who is surgery for? →NHS eligibility →What the NHS pathway looks like →Private UK route →Private cost reality →Benefits →Risks →Recovery →Lifelong follow-up →Surgery vs medication →Surgery vs lifestyle-first →Psychological readiness →Questions to ask →Shift Says →Printable checklist →FAQs →Sources → The 30-second answer Bariatric surgery is not “the easy way out”. It is a major medical treatment for obesity that changes the stomach and, depending on the operation, sometimes the route food takes through the intestine. It can produce substantial and durable weight loss for appropriately selected people, but it also creates lifelong nutritional, behavioural and medical responsibilities. The right question is not “is surgery extreme?” It is “does the likely health benefit outweigh the surgical and lifelong trade-offs for me?” What is bariatric / metabolic surgery? Bariatric surgery is an umbrella term for operations used to treat severe obesity and related health problems. Modern services increasingly use the term metabolic surgery because the effects are not purely mechanical. Surgery can change hunger, satiety, gut hormones, blood-glucose regulation and the way food is digested. The NHS describes the main current procedures as sleeve gastrectomy, gastric bypass, gastric band, gastric balloon and endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty. Not all are equivalent: some permanently remove stomach tissue, some reroute the intestine, some use implanted devices, and some are endoscopic rather than conventional surgery. Who might reasonably consider surgery? Surgery enters the conversation when obesity is severe enough that the likely health gains can justify an operation and lifelong follow-up. Examples include people with very high BMI, significant type 2 diabetes, sleep apnoea, high blood pressure, mobility-limiting joint disease or repeated major weight regain despite appropriate non-surgical treatment. It can also be relevant when the amount of weight that needs to be lost to materially improve health is greater than someone has been able to sustain with lifestyle or medication alone. Who can get weight-loss surgery on the NHS? NHS public guidance says surgery may be available if BMI is 40 or above, or 35–40 with a condition likely to improve with weight loss, alongside willingness to make lifestyle changes and attend regular follow-up. Lower BMI thresholds can apply for people from South Asian, Chinese, other Asian, Middle Eastern, Black African or African-Caribbean backgrounds because obesity-related risk occurs at a lower BMI. NICE also says expedited assessment should be considered for some adults with recent-onset type 2 diabetes at lower BMI thresholds. Eligibility is not the same as automatic surgery. Referral leads to specialist assessment. Fitness for anaesthesia, previous treatment, nutrition, psychological readiness, smoking, expectations and ability to engage with lifelong follow-up all matter. What does the NHS pathway usually involve? GP / specialist referral Specialist weight-management assessment MDT review Surgery preparation Lifelong follow-up The exact route varies locally. A bariatric multidisciplinary team may include surgeons, physicians, specialist nurses, dietitians, psychologists and anaesthetic teams. The purpose is not to “make you prove you deserve surgery”; it is to reduce preventable risk and work out whether the operation and type of operation fit your circumstances. What if I go private in the UK? Private treatment can reduce waiting time and give more choice of surgeon or hospital, but you still need proper multidisciplinary assessment and aftercare. The operation itself is only one part of the package. Before comparing quotes, ask what is included: surgeon, anaesthetist, hospital stay, pre-op tests, dietitian, psychology input, emergency readmission arrangements, routine follow-up, blood monitoring and what happens if you develop a late complication. What does private surgery cost? Compare packages in our UK and Europe surgery cost guide. As a current benchmark, Ramsay quotes UK gastric sleeve packages from roughly £10,495 with 24 months of aftercare, while Spire examples vary by hospital and can exceed £12,000–£13,000. Prices change, so we treat them as examples, not market-wide guarantees. A lower sticker price can become expensive if aftercare, complications, revision, flights or emergency treatment are excluded. Bariatric surgery is one purchase where “what happens after?” matters as much as “how much today?”. What can surgery potentially improve? For appropriately selected people, substantial weight loss can improve mobility, type 2 diabetes control, high blood pressure, sleep apnoea, quality of life and other obesity-related disease. The benefit is individual and depends on starting health, procedure, follow-up and long-term behaviour. It can also change daily life in less clinical ways: fitting comfortably in seats, walking without pain, playing with children, exercising and reducing the constant effort required to manage severe hunger or portion size. What are the trade-offs and risks? Short-term surgical risks Bleeding Infection Blood clots Anaesthetic complications Leak from staple/join lines Readmission Long-term considerations Nutritional deficiencies Reflux or digestive symptoms depending on procedure Gallstones Loose skin Weight regain Need for revision surgery in some people Lifelong monitoring Risk varies significantly by operation, individual health and surgical centre. A good service should discuss its own complication and follow-up arrangements rather than quoting generic reassurance. What is recovery like? The NHS says people usually leave hospital around 1–3 days after weight-loss surgery and start returning toward normal activities after around 4–6 weeks. Procedure and individual recovery differ. Food progresses gradually from fluids to purée/runny foods, soft foods and then a balanced solid diet. This staged approach protects healing tissue while you learn how your altered stomach responds. The bit that should be written in capital letters: lifelong follow-up Weight-loss surgery does not finish at hospital discharge. NHS guidance describes regular follow-up for life, with specialist bariatric clinic input usually for at least the first two years followed by ongoing annual review in primary care. Monitoring can include blood tests for vitamin and mineral deficiencies, physical health review, diet/activity support and psychological support. Supplements are often lifelong, with exact requirements dependent on the procedure and specialist advice. Surgery vs weight-loss medication SurgeryMedication Intervention One major procedure with permanent or semi-permanent anatomical change Ongoing medicine while treatment is used Up-front risk Higher because it involves anaesthesia and surgery No operation, but medicine-specific risks/side effects Follow-up Lifelong nutritional/clinical follow-up Ongoing prescribing and treatment review Stopping You cannot simply “stop” a sleeve Medication can be stopped, but weight regain can occur Best choice? Depends on severity, health risk, previous treatment, preference, affordability and clinical suitability. Surgery vs lifestyle-first Lifestyle change is not an alternative you “fail” before being allowed a proper treatment. Nutrition, movement, sleep and behaviour remain important before and after surgery. But severe obesity is a chronic biological condition, and lifestyle alone may not produce enough durable weight loss for everyone. The question is whether structured non-surgical treatment has a realistic chance of delivering enough benefit within a sensible timeframe — not whether you can prove enough willpower. The psychological side of surgery Surgery changes eating, body size, relationships with food, social situations and sometimes identity. It does not automatically remove emotional eating, binge triggers, low mood or unrealistic expectations. Pre-operative psychological assessment can identify areas needing support. That should be viewed as protection, not a barrier. Questions to ask a bariatric service Which operation do you recommend for me and why? How many of these operations does the surgeon perform? What are your leak, readmission and revision rates? Who manages complications outside normal hours? How long is dietitian follow-up included? What blood tests will I need for life? Which vitamins will I need? What if I develop reflux? What if I regain weight? What is your policy on revision surgery? What happens if I become pregnant? What support exists for excess skin or body-image issues? Shift Says Our take Surgery should not be treated as failure and it should not be treated as a quick fix. For the right person it can be one of the most effective tools available for severe obesity. We would compare it against medication, NHS support and a properly structured lifestyle route — then choose based on health benefit, risk, durability and what you can realistically live with long term. Printable surgery decision checklist I understand why surgery is being considered in my case. I have compared more than one procedure. I understand NHS and private routes. I know the key short-term risks. I understand lifelong vitamin/blood-test follow-up. I have compared surgery with medication and lifestyle options. I know who will look after me if something goes wrong. I understand that weight regain can still happen.Print / Save FAQs Is weight-loss surgery available on the NHS? Yes for eligible people after specialist assessment; BMI, obesity-related health conditions and ability to engage with follow-up all matter. Is bariatric surgery reversible? It depends on the procedure. A sleeve removes stomach tissue and is not simply reversible; a band can be removed; ESG does not remove the stomach. How long is recovery? The NHS says many people begin returning to normal activities after around 4–6 weeks, though this varies. Do I need vitamins for life? Long-term supplementation and blood monitoring are standard after bariatric surgery; exact needs depend on the operation and your bariatric team. Can weight come back after surgery? Yes. Surgery is powerful but not immunity from weight regain. Is surgery better than Mounjaro? There is no universal winner. They have different risks, durability, costs and suitability. title: The Complete Walking Guide for Men
description: A useful walking plan starts from what you can comfortably do now. Make the route, timing and pace repeatable before chasing a step total. Walking can support fitness and wellbeing; the scales are not the only way to tell whether the routine is helping.
keywords: Home / Knowledge Centre / Lifestyle / The Complete Walking Guide for Men Cornerstone guide The Complete Walking Guide for Men A useful walking plan starts from what you can comfortably do now. Make the route, timing and pace repeatable before chasing a step total. Walking can support fitness and wellbeing; the scales are not the only way to tell whether the routine is helping. Find a starting route Choose a familiar route with a safe surface, an easy way home and somewhere to pause if needed. Try a manageable outing and notice how you feel during it and afterwards. If walking is limited by an injury, illness, balance problem or breathlessness you are concerned about, ask for individual advice about suitable activity. Understand pace without buying a gadget The NHS describes brisk walking as a pace where you can still talk but cannot sing. You do not have to start there. Begin at a comfortable pace and build as appropriate. A watch's calorie estimate or an arbitrary step target should not dictate what is safe or useful for your body. Use a small plan you can actually repeat Choose a realistic slot, such as after lunch on three days this week. Keep the first route short enough that a busy day does not make it impossible. Record whether you went and how the outing felt, rather than only the distance. If the routine feels manageable, increase one part gradually. There is no need to add speed, hills and distance together. Know the broader activity guidance The updated UK Chief Medical Officers' guidance recommends adults work towards at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, or an appropriate equivalent, and muscle-strengthening activity on at least two days. Some activity is better than none. Walking is one part of that picture; it does not automatically cover strength or balance needs. Make room for real life Use the route for something you already do: a short errand, a break from your desk or a chat with a friend. Plan an alternative for darkness or poor weather. Comfortable footwear and a route you trust are more useful than buying equipment that never leaves the cupboard. Adapt the routine to your access and circumstances. Do not push through warning symptoms Stop if movement brings concerning symptoms or significant pain, and get appropriate medical advice. Sudden persistent chest pain or a medical emergency needs 999. A walking plan is not an assessment of heart or lung disease, and this guide does not replace advice about restrictions after illness, injury or an operation. Look for progress you can notice After a few weeks, compare how repeatable the routine has become, whether the same route feels easier and what gets in the way. If the plan keeps failing, shorten it or change the timing. If symptoms are worsening, seek assessment. Progress is a workable routine you can return to, rather than one impressive day followed by nothing. title: Orforglipron (Foundayo) UK: Definitive Oral GLP-1 Guide
description: A UK-focused guide to Foundayo (orforglipron): MHRA authorisation, daily dosing, ATTAIN evidence, safety, access and comparisons with oral Wegovy and Mounjaro.
keywords: Home / Orforglipron (Foundayo) UK: Definitive Oral GLP-1 Guide Current UK Medicine Decision Guide Orforglipron (Foundayo) UK: Definitive Oral GLP-1 Guide Written and researched by Matt O’Brien, founder of Shift Some Timber. Updated 26 August 2026UK-focusedMHRA-authorised in the UK Jump to what mattersWhere it stands now →What is Orforglipron? →Why the oral format matters →ATTAIN Phase 3 evidence →US approval: Foundayo →What about the UK? →Side effects & safety →Cost and access →Orforglipron vs oral Wegovy →Orforglipron vs Mounjaro →Who might prefer it? →Questions you haven't thought to ask →Shift Says →Printable summary →FAQs →Sources → Orforglipron has crossed an important line Foundayo is now an authorised UK prescription medicine. The MHRA authorised orforglipron under the brand Foundayo on 10 August 2026 for weight management and type 2 diabetes in defined adult populations. It is prescription-only; authorisation does not mean automatic NHS access or that it is suitable for everyone. What is Orforglipron? Orforglipron is a small-molecule, non-peptide GLP-1 receptor agonist taken once daily by mouth. Unlike peptide-based oral semaglutide, its design allows it to be taken without the same fasting and water restrictions highlighted in Lilly's US product positioning. That could make adherence easier for people who want GLP-1 treatment without injections or complicated morning routines. Why does a straightforward GLP-1 pill matter? No injection Removes needle aversion and cold-chain injection logistics. Daily habit Some people prefer a daily tablet; others prefer a weekly injection they can forget about. Manufacturing scale A small-molecule oral medicine may have different manufacturing and distribution economics from peptide injections. What did the ATTAIN Phase 3 Shift Programme show? In ATTAIN-1, adults with obesity or overweight without diabetes taking the highest studied dose lost an average of about 12.4% of body weight at 72 weeks in Lilly's reported efficacy analysis. The Shift Programme also includes people with type 2 diabetes and maintenance studies. The headline percentage is lower than top-dose figures reported for some injectable medicines, but efficacy is only one part of the decision. Convenience, price, tolerability and willingness to stay on treatment can matter just as much in real life. Foundayo: what US approval tells us FDA approval means the treatment has moved beyond “future medicine” status in the United States. Lilly launched Foundayo with once-daily dosing and US direct-to-patient pricing. For a UK reader, the important change is that Foundayo now has an MHRA-authorised indication and UK product instructions. Access, prescribing suitability, private availability and any future NHS recommendation remain separate questions. Is Orforglipron approved in the UK? Yes. The MHRA authorised Foundayo on 10 August 2026 for weight loss and weight maintenance in adults with a BMI of 30 or above, or a BMI from 27 to below 30 with at least one weight-related comorbidity, alongside a reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity. It is also authorised for insufficiently controlled type 2 diabetes. Individual suitability requires assessment by a qualified prescriber. Important: MHRA authorisation confirms the medicine may be prescribed within its authorised indications. It does not guarantee NHS availability, private stock or individual suitability. Side effects and safety Lilly's Phase 3 Shift Programme described a safety and tolerability profile broadly consistent with GLP-1 medicines, with gastrointestinal effects such as nausea, diarrhoea, vomiting and constipation among the important practical issues. UK prescribing and safety information should be checked against the current MHRA-approved product information and Patient Information Leaflet. What might it cost in the UK? Foundayo is now authorised and has begun appearing through UK private providers, but retail prices can change by dose and provider. Shift does not publish a treatment price until its regulated supply and commercial partners are confirmed. NHS availability is separate from MHRA authorisation and depends on NICE and commissioning decisions. Private prices should be dated, sourced and checked for consultation, delivery and subscription conditions. Orforglipron vs oral Wegovy Orforglipron / FoundayoOral Wegovy Molecule Small-molecule GLP-1 agonist Semaglutide peptide Route Daily tablet Daily tablet Food/water restrictions MHRA states it can be taken at any time, without food or water restrictions Follow approved UK semaglutide tablet instructions UK status MHRA-authorised in the UK on 10 August 2026 MHRA approved oral Wegovy for weight management in June 2026 Orforglipron vs Mounjaro Mounjaro generally offers stronger average weight-loss efficacy in its obesity trial Shift Programme but requires weekly injection. Orforglipron's attraction is a convenient oral GLP-1 format. For some people the extra efficacy of an injection may matter more; for others a pill they will actually take consistently may win. Who might eventually prefer Orforglipron? People who strongly dislike injections. People who prefer a daily medication routine. People for whom storage and travel with injectable medicines is inconvenient. People who want GLP-1 therapy but value simplicity enough to accept potentially lower average weight loss than stronger injectable options. Questions you haven't thought to ask yet Would I remember a daily pill more reliably than a weekly injection? Will UK pricing actually be cheaper? Will NHS criteria differ from injectable medicines? How will oral Wegovy affect its UK positioning? What happens if I miss several daily doses? Would lower average efficacy still be enough for my health goals? Shift Says Our take Orforglipron could be a big deal because convenience is a clinical feature, not just a marketing feature. A treatment somebody will reliably take can beat a theoretically stronger option they hate using. The UK authorisation is now confirmed. The next questions are access, price, individual suitability and how a daily tablet compares with weekly injections in real life. Printable summary Orforglipron checklist Once-daily oral small-molecule GLP-1. FDA-approved in the US as Foundayo in April 2026. MHRA-authorised in the UK on 10 August 2026. ATTAIN-1 reported around 12.4% average weight loss at the highest dose. Convenience may be a major differentiator.Print / Save FAQs Is Orforglipron a pill? Yes. It is a once-daily oral small-molecule GLP-1 receptor agonist. Is Orforglipron approved? Foundayo is authorised in both the US and UK; the MHRA granted UK authorisation on 10 August 2026. Is Foundayo available in the UK? Yes. The MHRA authorised Foundayo in the UK on 10 August 2026. It is prescription-only and individual suitability must be assessed. How much weight did people lose? ATTAIN-1 reported about 12.4% average weight reduction at the highest dose at 72 weeks. Does it need injections? No. Is it the same as oral Wegovy? No. Both are oral GLP-1 medicines, but they are different molecules with different pharmacology and product instructions. Take the next useful step → Before you use the calculator What is this calculator for? Walking is one of the most accessible ways to increase daily activity. A walking calorie calculator estimates how much energy you may use during a walk based on your body weight, time, pace and sometimes distance. It is useful for understanding activity in context, but the number should never become a reason to 'earn' food or punish yourself for eating. What it measures Body weight Walking duration Pace or distance Estimated calories used Why it is here It can help you compare different walks, understand the value of regular movement and see how small bouts of activity add up over a week. What this result cannot tell you No calculator can understand everything about you. Important limitations include: Terrain Weather Fitness level Walking efficiency Heart rate Carrying weight Individual metabolism Accuracy of pace estimates Shift Says The best walk is the one you actually do. Ten minutes with the dog still counts. You do not need a mountain, Lycra or a spreadsheet. How to use the result sensibly Use the number as a starting point. How are you feeling? → Explore related Knowledge → Take the Health MOT → Register to Shift Some Timber → How this works, limitations & evidence Interpretation, limitations & evidence Understand the result — then decide what matters This calculator uses MET values for different walking intensities. METs are a standard way to estimate the energy cost of activity, but real calorie burn varies with pace, hills, fitness, body composition and walking efficiency. How the calculation works Estimate Calories ≈ MET × 3.5 × body weight (kg) ÷ 200 × minutes. The pace options use approximate MET values. Hills, load, terrain and individual efficiency can change the real energy cost. The health benefit is bigger than the calorie number NHS guidance recommends at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity activity a week for adults aged 19 to 64; brisk walking can contribute to that total. Even a brisk 10-minute daily walk has health benefits and counts toward the weekly total. How do I know whether a walk is brisk? A practical NHS test is that you can still talk but would struggle to sing. If you can comfortably sing, the walk is likely lighter intensity. Do not eat back the estimate automatically Exercise calorie estimates can be wrong in either direction. If your goal is fat loss, treat walking as part of your activity plan rather than as a voucher for extra food. Build progression without wrecking your knees Add one variable at a time: minutes, pace, frequency or hills. If you are currently sedentary, adding 10 minutes regularly is a real progression. Walking plus strength beats walking alone Walking builds aerobic activity; strength training helps preserve muscle and function. The UK guideline includes both aerobic activity and strengthening work on at least two days per week. Common questions Is the calorie estimate exact? No. MET-based calculations are population estimates. Does slow walking count? Yes as movement; brisker walking is more likely to meet moderate-intensity criteria. Is walking enough for health? It is an excellent foundation, but strength work is also recommended. What should I use next? NICE recommends it particularly for adults with BMI under 35. How the ratio works Waist-to-height ratio = waist circumference ÷ height, using the same units for both. Example: 90 cm waist ÷ 180 cm height = 0.50. NICE interpretation RatioNICE interpretation 0.40–0.49 Healthy central adiposity / no increased risk from this measure 0.50–0.59 Increased health risk 0.60+ Further increased health risk The simple message is: aim to keep your waist less than half your height. How to measure consistently Use a flexible tape on bare skin, keep it level and measure in the same anatomical position each time. For personal tracking, consistency is more useful than chasing millimetre precision. Why waist matters Higher central adiposity is associated with increased risk of type 2 diabetes, hypertension and cardiovascular disease. Waist therefore gives information that body weight alone cannot. When the ratio is especially useful It can add context when BMI is borderline, when weight changes slowly but waist is falling, or where high muscle mass makes BMI harder to interpret. Do not obsess over millimetres Tape placement, breathing and time of day can create variation. Review trends over weeks rather than repeatedly re-measuring until you get the number you want. A pint is not “one unit” and a glass of wine is not automatically one unit either. How UK alcohol units are calculated Formula Units = volume in millilitres × ABV (%) ÷ 1,000. Example: 568 ml pint × 4% ÷ 1,000 = 2.27 units. What does the UK guideline say? NHS guidance advises men and women not to regularly drink more than 14 units a week to keep health risks from alcohol low. If you regularly drink 14 units, spread drinking over 3 or more days and include drink-free days. Why counting 'drinks' is unreliable A strong craft beer, large wine and double spirit can contain very different units. Size and ABV matter. Alcohol and weight management Alcohol contains energy, can lower food restraint, disrupt sleep and often arrives alongside higher-calorie food. Cutting back can improve a weight-management week in more ways than the drink calories alone. Alcohol and GLP-1 medicines There is no single blanket rule for everybody, but alcohol may worsen nausea, reflux or dehydration in some people taking weight-loss medication. Individual medical conditions and medicines matter too. When cutting down needs medical help If you are dependent on alcohol, stopping suddenly can be dangerous. Seek clinical advice rather than using this calculator as a detox plan. NHS: alcohol dependence and withdrawal. Common questions Is one pint one unit? Usually not. A 568 ml pint at 4% is about 2.3 units. Can I save 14 units for Saturday? NHS guidance advises spreading drinking over 3 or more days if you regularly drink up to 14 units. Do alcohol-free drinks count? Very low or alcohol-free products usually contribute little or no alcohol, but check the label. What should I use next? It is used widely in healthcare because it gives a quick, consistent way to estimate whether somebody falls within broad weight categories that may be associated with different levels of health risk. It is widely used by NHS and NICE services, but it is a screening measure, not a diagnosis. How BMI is calculated Formula BMI = weight in kilograms ÷ height in metres². Example: 90 kg at 1.80 m gives 90 ÷ (1.80 × 1.80) = BMI 27.8. How to interpret an adult BMI BMIStandard adult classification Under 18.5 Below the standard healthy range 18.5–24.9 Healthy weight range 25–29.9 Overweight 30+ Obesity, with classes increasing as BMI rises For people from South Asian, Chinese, other Asian, Middle Eastern, Black African or African-Caribbean backgrounds, NHS/NICE use lower thresholds for increased cardiometabolic risk: overweight starts at 23 and obesity at 27.5. Where BMI is useful Screening It helps identify people who may benefit from a wider health assessment. Treatment pathways BMI is still used in NHS medication and bariatric-surgery criteria, usually alongside health conditions. Tracking For one person over time, falling BMI generally reflects falling body weight at the same height. Where BMI falls short BMI cannot distinguish fat from muscle, cannot show where fat is stored and does not directly measure fitness, blood pressure, glucose, cholesterol or wellbeing. A muscular person can have a high BMI without high body fat; another person can have a lower BMI but high central adiposity. Use waist-to-height ratio alongside it NICE recommends waist-to-height ratio as an additional measure of central adiposity in adults with BMI under 35. A practical public-health message is to keep your waist to less than half your height. Ratios of 0.5–0.59 indicate increased risk and 0.6+ further increased risk. Protein is essential for maintaining muscle, supporting recovery and helping you feel satisfied after meals. A protein calculator estimates a daily intake based on your body weight, activity and goals. It can be particularly useful during weight loss because preserving lean mass matters — especially if you are eating less overall or using a weight-management treatment that reduces appetite. What it measures Body weight Activity level Goal or context Estimated daily protein range Why it is here It can give you a sensible protein target to aim around rather than guessing or relying on gym-bro numbers that may be far more than you need. What this result cannot tell you No calculator can understand everything about you. Important limitations include: Kidney disease or other conditions requiring individual advice Your total calorie intake Protein quality and food choices Meal timing preferences How much you can comfortably eat Individual clinical advice Shift Says You do not need to live on shakes and chicken breasts. Look at the overall trend, how you feel, what is happening with your waist, movement, sleep, blood pressure and other relevant health markers. Where the result is unexpected, concerning or difficult to interpret, a qualified healthcare professional can put it into context. Industry-standard does not mean individually perfect. How are you feeling? → Explore related Knowledge → Take the Health MOT → Register to Shift Some Timber → How this works, limitations & evidence Interpretation, limitations & evidence Understand the result — then decide what matters The calculator multiplies body weight by the planning level you select. That is useful for building a target, but the number becomes less reliable when body weight is very high, because protein requirements do not always scale perfectly with excess body fat. What does the UK reference intake say? The UK adult reference nutrient intake for protein is based on roughly 0.75 g per kg of body weight per day for generally healthy adults. That is a population reference for adequacy — not necessarily an ideal target for somebody dieting hard, getting older or resistance training. Why this calculator starts higher The available planning levels — 1.2, 1.6 and 2.0 g/kg — are deliberately presented as planning options rather than medical prescriptions. Higher protein intakes are commonly used during calorie restriction and strength training to support satiety and lean tissue. What if the result looks enormous? Use common sense with high body weights. If a straight current-weight calculation produces a very large target that is difficult to eat or medically inappropriate, do not force it. A dietitian may use goal weight, reference weight or another method. Spread protein across the day For many people, three or four protein opportunities are easier than trying to rescue the target at 9pm. A practical day might include eggs or yoghurt at breakfast, chicken, tuna or beans at lunch, a protein-led dinner and one protein-rich snack. Consistency across ordinary meals is generally more useful than chasing a perfect number with late-night shakes. Protein on Mounjaro or Wegovy Reduced appetite can make it easier to miss protein altogether. Guy’s and St Thomas’ NHS uses practical targets around 80–100 g/day for many patients taking weight-loss medicines, alongside individual advice. Food first — shakes optional Protein shakes can be convenient but they are not required. Meat, fish, eggs, yoghurt, cottage cheese, beans, lentils, tofu and meat alternatives can all contribute. The target should fit normal food, your calorie intake and any medical advice you have been given. Common questions Is more protein always better? No. Once needs are met, ever-higher intakes do not automatically produce more fat loss or muscle. Do I need protein powder? No. It is convenience, not a requirement. What if I have kidney disease? Get individual clinical or dietetic advice before adopting a high-protein target. What should I use next? It uses the Mifflin–St Jeor resting-energy equation and then applies the activity level you select. Your real maintenance intake is the intake that holds average weight broadly stable over time. How the estimate is calculated Mifflin–St Jeor equation used for adult men Resting energy ≈ (10 × weight kg) + (6.25 × height cm) − (5 × age) + 5. The calculator then multiplies resting energy by the selected activity factor to estimate total daily energy expenditure. Body composition differs Two men of the same weight and height can have different energy expenditure. Life changes Work, illness, sleep, training and weight loss itself can change energy needs. Turning maintenance into a weight-loss target NHS Better Health commonly uses a reduction of around 600 kcal/day as a general population starting point for weight loss. That is not compulsory and can be too aggressive or too small for some people. Do not turn the calculator into a race to the lowest intake. A useful deficit still needs enough food for protein, fibre, micronutrients and a life you can sustain. How to calibrate the estimate with real life Use the estimate for 2–4 weeks. Track average weight under reasonably consistent conditions. If weight is stable, your logged average intake is probably close to maintenance. If weight is trending down or up, adjust gradually rather than making a huge change after three days. Why plateaus happen As body weight falls, energy needs usually fall. Activity can also drift down without you noticing, and portion sizes can creep up. A plateau does not prove your metabolism has stopped working. title: Testosterone and Weight in Men: Evidence and Testing
description: A careful guide to testosterone and weight in men: symptoms, obesity, sleep, testing and why online ‘low T’ diagnosis is not reliable.
keywords: MEN OVER 40 · TESTOSTERONE Testosterone and weight: do not diagnose yourself from an advert Low energy, reduced confidence, poorer sleep and changes in body composition can have many causes. Excess weight and testosterone can be connected, but symptoms alone cannot establish testosterone deficiency. Proper history, examination and correctly timed blood testing matter. Written and researched by Matt O’Brien. Evidence checked 2026-08-26. Part of the Shift authority systemWeight loss for men over 40 →Men's weight-management centre → Quick takeaways Symptoms are not specific to low testosterone. Obesity and sleep apnoea can be relevant. Weight loss may improve levels in some men. Testosterone treatment requires proper diagnosis and monitoring. Why the relationship is complicated Higher body fat can be associated with lower measured testosterone, while low testosterone can also affect muscle, energy and body composition. Illness, medicines, alcohol, sleep and ageing may contribute. One untimed test or an online symptom quiz is not a reliable diagnosis. Start with the wider health picture Discuss persistent sexual symptoms, reduced morning erections, marked fatigue or other concerns with a GP or appropriate clinician. Sleep apnoea, diabetes risk, depression, thyroid problems and medication effects may need consideration. Weight management can be part of improving health without pretending every symptom will disappear at a target weight. What weight loss may do Some men living with obesity see improved testosterone measures after meaningful weight loss. The response varies and does not prove that weight was the only issue. Strength activity, adequate nutrition and sleep support function, but supplements marketed as testosterone boosters should not replace assessment. Treatment is not a lifestyle accessory Testosterone therapy has indications, risks and monitoring requirements. It is not simply an energy product or shortcut to muscle. A qualified clinician should interpret symptoms and repeated blood results in context. Frequently asked questions Can belly fat lower testosterone? Higher body fat can be associated with lower testosterone measures, but the relationship is complex and requires proper assessment. Will weight loss definitely raise testosterone? It may improve levels in some men living with obesity, but results vary and symptoms may have other causes. title: Confidence, Weight and Feeling Like Yourself Again
description: Why health change can be about identity as much as a number. A practical, plain-English guide for UK men.
keywords: mind Confidence, Weight and Feeling Like Yourself Again Weight and confidence can become tangled together. A change on the scales may matter to you, but you do not have to put the rest of your life on hold until it happens. title: GLP-1 Side Effects: Nausea, Constipation and When to Get Help
description: A practical UK guide to common GLP-1 side effects including nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea and constipation, plus warning signs and prescriber support.
keywords: PRACTICAL GLP-1 SUPPORT GLP-1 side effects: common does not mean ignore everything Nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea and constipation are commonly reported with GLP-1 and related weight-management medicines. Part of the Shift authority systemWeight-loss injections for men →Weight-loss tablets for men → Quick takeaways Follow the prescribed dose schedule. Hydration and adequate intake matter. Do not copy somebody else's medication or side-effect remedy. Severe abdominal pain, repeated vomiting or dehydration need prompt help. The bits blokes actually talk about The official side-effect lists matter, but real life is usually less tidy. Matt’s own experience included nausea, stomach cramps and the dreaded “eggy breath”. For him those difficult bits settled, but that is one person’s experience — not a prediction of what will happen to you. If something is new, severe, persistent or getting worse, treat it as information for the service looking after your prescription rather than something you have to “push through”. Lived-experience context from Matt’s story. Clinical decisions still belong with the treating service. Eggy breath: what actually helps Those sulphur-smelling burps can be grim. A slowed-down stomach can make rich meals sit around longer, so the boring fixes are often the useful ones: eat smaller portions, eat more slowly, keep fluids going, and notice whether very fatty or heavy meals make it worse. Staying upright after eating can also be easier than flopping straight onto the sofa. Do not try to “tough it out” if the burps arrive with repeated vomiting, severe or persistent tummy pain, a swollen abdomen, or you cannot keep fluids down. Those are reasons to contact the service looking after your medicine or seek urgent medical help depending on severity. This is practical symptom support, not a diagnosis. If it keeps happening or is getting worse, tell your prescriber or pharmacist rather than endlessly changing food around it. Nausea and reduced appetite Smaller meals, slower eating and avoiding foods that clearly worsen symptoms may help some people. The aim is not to stop eating altogether. Regular inability to meet fluid or nutrition needs should be discussed with the treating service. Symptoms after a dose change are useful information for the prescriber; they are not a challenge to endure silently. Constipation Lower food intake, less fibre, dehydration and reduced movement can contribute. Fluids, appropriate fibre and activity may help, but advice must account for the individual and their other conditions or medicines. Persistent constipation, significant pain, vomiting or inability to pass stool or wind needs medical advice. Vomiting and diarrhoea Repeated vomiting or diarrhoea can cause dehydration. Follow sick-day advice relevant to your health and medicines, and contact the treating service where symptoms persist. Do not take extra doses after vomiting or alter the schedule without instructions. Missed dose, changed day or not sure what to do? There is not one universal GLP-1 missed-dose rule, so do not guess and do not double up. Mounjaro (tirzepatide) weekly injection: the UK leaflet says take the missed dose as soon as possible if it is 4 days or less late. If more than 4 days have passed, skip it and use the next dose on your usual day. Leave at least 3 days between doses. Wegovy (semaglutide) weekly injection: the UK leaflet says take it as soon as possible if it is 5 days or less late. If more than 5 days have passed, skip it and continue on the usual day. Wegovy tablets: if you forget a dose, skip it and take your normal dose the next day. Never take a double dose to make up for one you missed. The current leaflet for the exact product in your hand—and your prescriber or pharmacist—wins if anything here differs from your own instructions. Shift can help you organise food, fluids, movement and what to remember; it does not replace prescribing advice. Red flags Seek urgent medical help for severe or persistent abdominal pain, signs of serious dehydration, collapse, breathing difficulty, swelling suggesting an allergic reaction, or rapidly worsening symptoms. This page cannot determine whether a symptom is caused by the medicine. Frequently asked questions Is nausea normal on GLP-1 treatment? It is commonly reported, especially around dose escalation, but persistent, severe or worsening nausea should be discussed with the treating service. What helps constipation on GLP-1 medication? Fluids, suitable fibre and movement may help some people, but persistent or concerning symptoms require individual advice. title: Alcohol on GLP-1 Medication: A Practical UK Guide
description: A practical guide to alcohol while using GLP-1 weight-management medication: appetite, nausea, dehydration, calories and when to ask your prescriber.
keywords: PRACTICAL GLP-1 SUPPORT Alcohol on GLP-1 medication: no sermon, but do understand the trade-offs There is no useful universal answer of “never” or “carry on as normal”. Written and researched by Matt O’Brien. Evidence checked 2026-08-26. Part of the Shift authority systemWeight-loss injections for men →Weight-loss tablets for men → Quick takeaways Check your medicine information and prescriber advice. Alcohol may worsen gastrointestinal symptoms or dehydration. Drinking can reduce dietary control and sleep quality. Severe or persistent symptoms need appropriate advice. Why alcohol can feel different GLP-1 and related medicines can alter appetite and slow stomach emptying. Some people experience nausea, vomiting, reflux or reduced food intake. Alcohol on top of those effects may be harder to tolerate. Individual responses vary; somebody else's pub report is not a dosing instruction. The weight-management trade-off Alcohol contains energy and can make high-calorie food more likely. It can also disrupt sleep, which may affect hunger, energy and activity the next day. That does not make one drink a moral failure. It means frequency, quantity and what happens around drinking belong in the plan. A practical lower-risk approach Do not drink to test your tolerance immediately after a dose change or while you are already unwell. Eat and hydrate appropriately according to your treatment guidance, pace drinks and avoid pressure to match somebody else's intake. If alcohol has become the main way you cope with stress or sleep, that deserves support beyond calorie arithmetic. When to speak to the treating service Ask your prescriber or pharmacist if you have diabetes, liver or pancreatic disease, take medicines affected by alcohol, or have recurrent vomiting, severe abdominal pain or dehydration. Seek urgent medical help for severe or rapidly worsening symptoms. Frequently asked questions Is alcohol forbidden on Mounjaro or Wegovy? There is not one universal rule for every person. Check the current product information and ask the treating service about your health and other medicines. Can alcohol worsen nausea on GLP-1 treatment? It may worsen nausea, vomiting, reflux or dehydration for some people. title: Stress, Eating and Weight Gain in Men

You may skip meals when busy, graze after work, or reach for alcohol when the house finally goes quiet. For a few days, note the situation and what you needed at the time. You do not have to count every calorie to notice that lunch keeps disappearing. Prepare for the difficult hour If you usually arrive home ravenous, have something straightforward ready: leftovers, a sandwich, eggs on toast or another meal that suits your needs. title: Calories Explained Without the Nonsense
description: What calories are, why energy balance matters and why real life is more complicated than a slogan.
keywords: weight Calories explained without the nonsense Calories describe the energy in food and drink. Understanding them can make portions less confusing. You do not need to turn every meal into a maths exam. Home / Calories Explained Without the Nonsense On this page A guide is not your personal target Read the portion as well as the number Compare similar foods fairly Think across the day or week Try one useful check Keep the tool in its place Sources A guide is not your personal target The NHS gives 2,500 kcal a day as a guide for an average man. It also explains that needs vary with age, weight, height and activity. That number is not a universal weight-loss target, and a calculator gives an estimate rather than an exact daily requirement. Use the information to understand your usual meals. Individual dietary needs, medical conditions and treatment belong in a conversation with an appropriate qualified professional. Read the portion as well as the number On a food label, look for energy, usually shown in kcal and kJ. Nutrition information is given per 100g or 100ml, and sometimes per portion. The manufacturer's portion may be different from yours. Here is a made-up label to show the calculation. It is not a recommended meal size:What the label or packet saysEnergy Per 100g 160 kcal Whole packet: 350g 560 kcal Half the packet: 175g 280 kcal The whole-packet calculation is 160 × 3.5. If you eat half, that is half the packet's energy. Add anything you serve with it if you are keeping a record. The point is to understand what the number covers. A packet labelled as two servings does not become one serving because you opened it alone. Compare similar foods fairly The per-100g figure gives you a common starting point when comparing similar products. Then check the amount you expect to eat. Comparing one manufacturer's small serving with another's larger serving can be misleading. Look beyond calories too. Labels also give information about fat, saturated fat, carbohydrate, sugars, protein and salt. A lower energy number alone does not describe the whole food or tell you whether that meal suits your needs. Think across the day or week The NHS Eatwell Guide describes the balance of food groups across your overall diet. You do not have to reproduce its proportions at every meal: aim for balance across a day or even a week. For a practical planning example, look at tomorrow's lunch and dinner together. What are you already having? Where could vegetables, fruit or another food group fit into the wider day? Choose something you enjoy and can realistically prepare. These are planning questions, not a prescribed menu or a reason to add oil to a meal just to make it look balanced. Try one useful check Choose one packaged food you buy regularly. Read the per-100g figure, the packet weight and any stated serving size. Work out what the portion you usually eat contains. Write down one thing you learnt. If you are tracking, remember the things that can slip out of the record: drinks, dressings, cooking oil and extras. If you are not tracking, you can still use a label to understand a portion or compare two similar products. Keep the tool in its place Tracking is optional. If counting makes you anxious, restrictive or preoccupied with food, seek suitable professional advice rather than pushing harder at the numbers. Do not compensate for eating by skipping needed food or forcing exercise. If you have an eating-disorder history, discuss weight-loss tracking with an appropriate professional first. After trying an approach, ask: could I manage it on a busy day, was I adequately fed, and did it make an ordinary meal easier? If it creates more work than it solves, simplify it or ask for support. title: Sleep Apnoea, Snoring and Weight in Men
description: How weight and obstructive sleep apnoea can be connected, symptoms men should not dismiss, diagnosis, treatment and where weight management fits.
keywords: MEN OVER 40 · SLEEP Sleep apnoea, snoring and weight: tired is not always just busy Loud snoring, breathing pauses, choking noises and crushing daytime tiredness are easy to normalise. Obstructive sleep apnoea is common and treatable. Weight can be an important risk factor, but it is not the only cause and losing weight is not a substitute for assessment. Written and researched by Matt O’Brien. Evidence checked 2026-08-26. Part of the Shift authority systemWeight loss for men over 40 →Men's weight-management centre → Quick takeaways Snoring alone does not diagnose sleep apnoea. Witnessed pauses and daytime sleepiness deserve attention. Weight management may help but does not replace treatment. Driving while dangerously sleepy is a safety issue. What obstructive sleep apnoea is During obstructive sleep apnoea, the airway repeatedly narrows or closes during sleep. Breathing interruptions disturb sleep even when the person does not remember waking. Possible signs include loud snoring, gasping, witnessed pauses, morning headaches, poor concentration, irritability and marked daytime sleepiness. Where weight fits Excess weight—particularly around the neck and upper airway—can increase risk, but anatomy, age, alcohol and other factors can also contribute. Men who are not living with obesity can still have sleep apnoea. Weight loss may reduce severity for some people, while treatments such as CPAP or other specialist options may still be needed. Do not wait for perfect weight loss Speak to a GP if symptoms suggest sleep apnoea. Assessment may involve a sleep study. Delaying until you have lost weight can prolong impaired sleep and health risk. Better sleep may also make eating, mood and activity easier to manage, so the relationship can work in both directions. Immediate practical points Avoid using alcohol as a sleep aid. Discuss sedating medicines with the appropriate professional. Follow treatment consistently if diagnosed. If sleepiness affects driving or safety-critical work, follow medical and DVLA advice promptly. Frequently asked questions Does losing weight cure sleep apnoea? It may improve severity for some people but does not guarantee a cure or replace assessment and treatment. Is loud snoring enough to diagnose it? No. Snoring is common; diagnosis requires clinical assessment, often including a sleep study. title: Weight-Loss Plateau: What Men Should Check Before Panicking
description: Why weight loss slows or plateaus, how to check the trend, what practical factors matter and why medication dose changes are not a DIY response.
keywords: PRACTICAL WEIGHT SUPPORT Weight-loss plateau: annoying, normal and worth investigating properly A flat scale for a few days is not a plateau. Water, salt, food, bowel contents and training can hide fat loss temporarily. A genuine multi-week stall deserves a calm review—not punishment, starvation or an invented medication change. Written and researched by Matt O’Brien. Evidence checked 2026-08-26. Part of the Shift authority systemMen's weight-management centre →Compare weight-loss treatments → Quick takeaways Use several weeks of comparable measurements. Check waist and behaviour as well as weight. Energy needs can fall after weight loss. Medication changes belong with the prescriber. First establish whether it is real Compare a trend of regular weigh-ins under similar conditions. Look at waist, clothes and the routine. One heavy weekend or constipated week can move scale weight without representing equivalent fat gain. If the longer trend is still falling, there may be nothing to fix. The scale can stall while the rest of you is still moving A flat scale is one signal, not the whole verdict. Check three things together: weight trend, waist or clothes, and strength or movement. If your waist is still coming down, a belt notch has moved, or the same 20-minute session is getting easier, you have evidence that the week is not standing still. What to do this week: keep weigh-ins consistent rather than daily panic-weighing; take one waist measurement; do one repeatable strength session; keep protein and regular meals sensible; and look for the obvious drift—drinks, grazing, bigger portions, less walking—before slashing food. If all three signals have genuinely stalled for a few weeks, that is a useful review point. If you are using treatment, take that pattern to the treating service rather than changing dose yourself. Why progress slows A lighter body generally uses less energy, and earlier habits may gradually loosen. Portions creep, drinks return, movement falls or weekends widen. Sleep, stress, illness and medicines may also influence the picture. Plateaus are information, not proof that your body is broken. Run a two-week audit Record meals honestly, check drinks and extras, rebuild walking and keep strength work where suitable. Do not slash intake recklessly. Choose the smallest change likely to restart a sustainable deficit. If treatment is involved, review appetite, side effects, adherence and progress with the treating service. Know when maintenance is success After substantial loss, a period of stable weight may protect routine and strength. Not every month needs to set a new personal record. Revisit the reason for losing weight and whether another loss phase is appropriate for health and life. Frequently asked questions How long counts as a weight-loss plateau? There is no universal cut-off, but a few days is not enough. Review comparable measurements across several weeks. Does a plateau mean my GLP-1 dose should increase? No automatic conclusion follows. title: Meal prep for busy men: a two-meal plan for a busy week
description: Make two awkward meals easier with a realistic meal-prep plan for a busy week, a simple backup and practical food-storage guidance.
keywords: nutrition Meal prep for busy men: a two-meal plan for a busy week Meal prep starts with the point in your week when food becomes a nuisance. Pick two meals that usually catch you out, then make those easier. A useful first attempt might be one dinner with an extra portion and one lunch you can put together quickly. Home / Meal prep for busy men: a two-meal plan for a busy week On this page Choose two real moments Shop from your kitchen first Give each meal a different job Put storage into the plan Keep one easy alternative Check what actually helped Sources Next step You do not need a new personality, matching containers or a Sunday spent cooking food you will resent by Wednesday. You need a plan you are likely to use. Choose two real moments Look at the next few days before deciding what to cook. For example, Tuesday might mean getting home late, while Wednesday lunch usually means buying whatever is nearest. Those are two specific problems you can prepare for. Write them down: “Tuesday dinner” and “Wednesday lunch”. Check where you will be eating, whether there is a fridge and whether reheating is possible. A brilliant microwave lunch is less brilliant when your workplace has no microwave. If the week is unpredictable, choose one meal and a cupboard backup instead. Start at a size you can repeat. Shop from your kitchen first Open the fridge, freezer and cupboard. Make a short list of ingredients you can already use, then choose the meals. This is easier than buying a new set of ingredients for every recipe. An illustrative list could include beans, tinned tomatoes, frozen vegetables, potatoes and wholemeal bread. Add ingredients that suit your tastes, allergies and household. This is a planning example rather than a tested recipe or a prescribed diet. Think about how the meals fit into the wider week. The NHS Eatwell Guide describes balance across the day or week, rather than requiring every plate to match a diagram. Its food groups include vegetables, starchy foods and protein foods such as beans, fish, eggs and meat. Use that as context, not another task to mark yourself against. Give each meal a different job For the late dinner, choose something you already enjoy and know how to prepare. If it is suitable for batch cooking and freezing, make an extra portion when you next cook it. Label that portion so it has a clear purpose rather than becoming an unidentified object at the back of the freezer. Cook a meal you already like in a larger batch, if the recipe can be safely scaled, and freeze the extra portions. For lunch, keep the preparation simpler. You might plan a sandwich with a filling you like, a piece of fruit and something else that fits your appetite and dietary needs. You might prefer soup, or a portion of a suitable cooked meal. Choose what you will want to eat, and plan safe storage and transport. The two meals do not need to look identical. One can solve a time problem; the other can solve the problem of making a decision while hungry and busy. Put storage into the plan Food safety is part of preparation. Follow packet instructions and use-by dates. The Food Standards Agency guidance linked below advises cooling cooked food and refrigerating it within one to two hours, and eating refrigerated leftovers within 48 hours or freezing them if that will not be possible. It advises defrosting in the fridge and using food within 24 hours of complete defrosting. Different foods can have additional precautions; check the guidance relevant to what you are preparing. Decide where the food will go before cooking. Check there is room, use suitable containers and put the date on them. If a meal depends on remembering to take it to work, leave yourself a reminder where you will see it. Cooling, storage and reheating Follow the Food Standards Agency guidance on cooling, chilling and reheating. Cool cooked food promptly, refrigerate it within two hours and reheat leftovers only once until steaming hot throughout. Rice has specific storage precautions; use the linked guidance rather than applying a general rule to every ingredient. If you cannot use a portion within its safe storage time, freeze it promptly if suitable. Keep one easy alternative A backup is useful when the plan meets real life. Pick something you can make from ingredients you usually keep in. Write it down beside the two planned meals. The alternative should be easy enough to use on a difficult evening. title: Belly Fat in Men: Why It Happens and What Helps
description: Why men gain belly fat, what waist measurements mean, why spot reduction fails and which practical changes support overall fat loss and health.
keywords: MEN OVER 40 · BELLY FAT Belly fat in men: understand the risk without buying the nonsense Men often notice weight gain at the belt before anywhere else. That does not mean one food, one hormone or one missing abdominal exercise caused it. It means waist measurement can add useful health context—and that the solution is overall fat loss, not a gadget promising to melt one body part. Written and researched by Matt O’Brien. Evidence checked 2026-08-26. Part of the Shift authority systemWeight loss for men over 40 →Men's weight-management centre → Quick takeaways You cannot choose where fat leaves first. Waist-to-height ratio adds context alongside BMI. Alcohol, food portions, sleep and activity can all contribute. Track the waist trend, not daily noise. Why the middle matters Abdominal fat includes fat under the skin and visceral fat around internal organs. Higher central adiposity is associated with increased cardiometabolic risk. That is why NICE advises using waist-to-height ratio alongside BMI for many adults. A waist measure is a screening signpost, not a diagnosis or a verdict on somebody's character. Why men gain it Overall energy balance remains central, but daily life shapes it: less movement, larger portions, alcohol, poor sleep, stress and loss of muscle can combine gradually. Genetics influence where people tend to store fat. Claims that one hormone or food is always responsible oversimplify a complicated picture. Persistent symptoms or concerns about health deserve assessment rather than a supplement funnel. What actually reduces belly fat The reliable route is reducing overall body fat through a sustainable energy deficit, adequate nutrition and activity. Walking helps; strength work supports function and muscle; food and drink changes usually carry much of the energy difference. Abdominal exercises can strengthen the trunk but do not selectively burn the fat covering it. Measure without becoming obsessed Measure at the same point and under similar conditions, then review monthly. Pair the number with weight, blood pressure, fitness, sleep and how clothes fit. If your waist is changing slowly while strength and daily function improve, that is still useful progress. Frequently asked questions Can sit-ups burn belly fat? No. They can strengthen abdominal muscles, but fat loss cannot be targeted to one body area. Is waist more useful than BMI? They answer different questions. BMI estimates weight relative to height; waist-to-height ratio adds information about central adiposity. Quick takeaways A plain-English introduction to semaglutide for weight management. The useful answer is usually more nuanced than one number or one rule. Use this information to guide your next step, not to diagnose yourself. What is actually going on? Modern prescription weight-management medicines can reduce appetite and support weight loss for eligible people, but they are medicines rather than casual lifestyle products. Current UK pathways require assessment, appropriate prescribing and follow-up. Wegovy is the brand name for semaglutide used for weight management. It acts through the GLP-1 pathway and is prescribed within specific indications. There is also a difference between what is possible in a controlled study and what is sustainable on a wet Wednesday after work. Evidence matters, but it has to be translated into a plan a normal person can repeat. What can you do about it? Use only medicine prescribed for you by a legitimate healthcare professional. Give the prescriber an accurate medical and medication history. Follow the dosing plan rather than copying somebody else's. Keep nutrition, hydration, movement and strength in the plan. Report persistent or worrying side effects to the treating service. You do not need to implement every point tomorrow. Pick the one or two changes most likely to improve your week. If they become normal, add the next layer. That usually works better than changing everything at once and being fed up by Friday. What people often get wrong Prescription treatment is neither cheating nor magic. It can help some people and be unsuitable for others. Another mistake is treating a health marker as a character judgement. BMI, waist size, calories, blood pressure and weight are measurements. They can be useful and sometimes important, but none tells you whether you are a good dad, a reliable mate or someone who has already made huge progress. When should you get proper medical advice? If you have persistent or worsening symptoms, unusually high or low readings, unexplained weight change, significant fatigue, chest pain, fainting, severe breathlessness, concerns about medication or a health condition that could affect diet or exercise, speak to an appropriate healthcare professional. Prescription weight-management treatment should only be used following proper assessment and prescribing. title: Stopping GLP-1 Treatment
description: What can happen after stopping GLP-1 treatment, including appetite return, weight regain, muscle considerations and practical maintenance planning.
keywords: PRACTICAL GLP-1 SUPPORT Stopping GLP-1 treatment: plan for appetite, not just the final injection Stopping is not a moral test. Appetite can return and weight regain is common in follow-up research. That does not mean everybody follows the same path or that treatment has failed. It means maintenance needs planning before the medicine disappears from the routine. Written and researched by Matt O’Brien. Evidence checked 2026-08-26. Part of the Shift authority systemCompare weight-loss treatments →Men's weight-management centre → Quick takeaways Do not change prescribed treatment without speaking to the treating service. Appetite and weight may change after stopping. Weight regain is biology, not proof of weak character. Food, activity, support and follow-up should be planned early. What research shows Recent evidence reviews show that people often regain weight after weight-management medicines are stopped, with faster regain reported after newer incretin treatments than after behavioural programmes. Study averages do not predict an individual's outcome. The evidence also reinforces that obesity commonly needs long-term management rather than a short contest with a finish line. Why appetite may feel louder The medicine's appetite effects reduce after stopping. Hunger, food thoughts and portion pressure may return. That can feel dramatic after months of quieter appetite. Expecting this response helps remove shame and makes practical planning more likely. What coming off can feel like in real life The change is not only a number on the scales. Food noise can feel louder again. Portions can become harder to judge. A routine that felt automatic can suddenly need thought. That can knock confidence, especially if you had started to feel “sorted”. Matt’s own weight-loss journey taught him that weight shows up in more than kilos: clothes, photographs, confidence, movement, energy and the things you quietly stop doing. Those are worth protecting too. Coming off should therefore be a support plan, not simply the date of the final dose. Build the landing before stopping Discuss the reason for stopping, timing, other health conditions and what follow-up is available. Make regular meals, protein, fibre, sleep and activity easier before appetite rises. Use regular but not obsessive monitoring. A small upward movement can trigger an early review rather than an all-or-nothing restart. Set the ordinary stuff up before you need it: meals you will actually eat, a short movement option for bad days, a check-in that remembers what has changed, and a human route when you need one. Keep a simple record of what treatment you were using, what has changed, any symptoms you are worried about and the questions you need answered. Contact the service that prescribed or dispensed the medicine; if you cannot reach them, use an appropriate NHS route for medical advice. Do not make up a taper or dose plan yourself. Shift’s job around that is different: keep food, movement, progress and headspace joined up so you are not starting from zero while the clinical question is being sorted. The head stuff counts as part of the plan Coming off can bring relief, worry, frustration or a fear that old habits will come rushing back. None of that needs turning into a motivational speech. Use the same rule as the rest of Shift: notice what is actually happening, make the next useful move and get a human involved when you need one. Review what changed, what support is missing and whether another evidence-based route is appropriate. Any future medicine decision belongs with a qualified prescriber.
